#6260. Latino Democrats celebrate midterm gains, with warning for party

California Rep. Linda T. Sánchez, here at a 2020 news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center, is the chair of BOLD PAC. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Latino voters moved sharply away from Republicans this year, and a record number of Latino Democratic candidates were elected.

But California Rep. Linda T. Sánchez has a warning for her fellow Democrats.

“Latino voters gave Democrats a two-year lease, but it expires in 2028 unless the party changes its playbook for good,” said Sánchez, who leads the campaign arm of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus.

Failure to address rising costs and push back against President Donald Trump’s immigration agenda could once again scramble the political calculus and spark another realignment in two years, said House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar of California.

“While Latinos shifted towards Democrats and … gave us this mandate as a party, Democrats must continue to earn their trust, not just every two years, but every single day,’’ he said.

Leaders of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus joined newly elected Latino members on Tuesday for a news conference to celebrate the recent wins and the role the group played in securing the House majority for Democrats. The caucus will boast 55 members in the next Congress, its largest roster ever, according to Sánchez.

BOLD PAC, the caucus’ campaign arm, invested heavily in Latino candidates this year, including in primaries.

California Rep. Salud Carbajal noted that BOLD PAC raised more than $18.5 million this cycle, which helped candidates leverage outside money.

Working-class majority-Latino districts in South Texas, Arizona and California were among the areas that provided Democrats with their biggest wins. Democrats capitalized on voter dissatisfaction over rising costs, the very issue that helped Trump and the GOP make significant gains among Hispanic voters just two years earlier.

But the wins weren’t limited to districts with sizable Latino populations.

Rep.-elect Denise Powell, who flipped a swing seat in Nebraska, credited BOLD PAC for playing a key role in her win.

“Yes, there are Latinos in Omaha, and those Latinos actually helped decide this race,’’ she said. “BOLD believed in me as a candidate, but they also believed in our community.”

Rep.-elect Bobby Pulido, who came to politics after a successful career as a Latin Grammy-winning Tejano singer, flipped a redrawn South Texas border district that Trump would have carried by 18 points in 2024.

“A lot of people feel like they don't belong to either party. But there's one thing about Latinos is we belong to each other,’’ Pulido said. “It's very hard to be a Latino right now in this country. … I expect to see us united, more united than ever, because it's a tough time right now.”

Several of the winning candidates deployed novel strategies to reach voters. Pulido famously began performing at quinceañeras after his Republican opponent dismissed him as a performer.

Colorado Rep.-elect Manny Rutinel, who flipped a battleground district north of Denver, attended World Cup and Broncos watch parties. “If people don't hear our message, then it doesn't matter,’’ he said.

The candidates “met those voters where they were,’’ Sánchez said. “They went into those communities and interacted in a very real and meaningful way. That's something I think that strategists or consultants don't always get. It's not just about pumping out lots of television commercials.”

Amid those successes for Latino Democrats, Florida, home to one of the largest Latino electorates in the country, was a different story. Republicans held all three majority-Latino districts in the Sunshine State, though former news anchor Eliott Rodriguez, the son of Cuban immigrants, came within half a percentage point of unseating GOP Rep. María Elvira Salazar in a district that backed Trump by 15 points in 2024.

BOLD PAC did have a victory to celebrate in Florida, with Rep. Darren Soto, the deputy chair of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus, narrowly prevailing in a district that Republicans redrew as one that no longer had a Latino majority.

“The redistricting wars ended up failing because of the investment by BOLD PAC,’’ Soto said.

#6259. Why United Airlines Doesn't Want Its Airbus A320s Anymore

Many US airlines are now modernizing their fleet by switching to more efficient and sustainable jets. United is not an exception and is currently accelerating a fleet modernization that will soon make one of its most familiar workhorses, the A320, a rare sight in its livery. But why this jet?

Once a reliable staple of the domestic network, the A320ceo family is now showing its age against a backdrop of rising fuel costs, maintenance demands, and heightened customer expectations. This is more than just a retirement story: it’s a shift in how United approaches capacity, efficiency, and consistency across its narrowbody operations

For aviation enthusiasts and frequent flyers, the news is notable because United’s A320s represent a significant part of its Airbus footprint, despite the airline’s image as a 'Boeing airline.' According to Planespotters.net, the carrier has 59 A320-200s in service and two parked, with an average age of 26.7 years, making them among the oldest active Airbus narrowbodies in the mainline fleet.

United’s A320-200s have been a common sight in the fleet for nearly three decades. With an average age of more than 26 years old, they are well into the late stages of a typical mainline narrowbody's service life. Older narrowbodies like the A320ceo require more frequent maintenance checks, from heavy structural inspections to engine overhauls.

United has already spent heavily to keep them flying, and CEO Scott Kirby told ch-aviation that the airline spent $100 million on engine work in 2024 alone, prompting the decision to retire 21 aircraft in 2025. While Kirby didn’t specify the types in his interview, we can deduce that the A320 is one of the candidates, alongside the Boeing 757, as the oldest airframes reach between 25 and 30 years of age.

As such, as reported by ch-aviation, United earmarked at least 17 of the oldest Airbus A320s in the fleet for retirement between August and October of 2025. For United, the problem isn’t just technical reliability but opportunity cost. Every dollar spent keeping a 30-year-old A320 flying is a dollar not invested in a fuel-efficient, higher-capacity replacement. As the A321neo order stream accelerates, keeping these older aircraft makes less and less financial sense.

Aircraft economics drive fleet decisions as much as mechanical limits. The A321neo offers a significant reduction in cost per available seat mile compared to the A320ceo, primarily due to its newer engines. The new aircraft carries more passengers, often 25–30% more in United’s configuration, while burning less fuel per seat.

This is thanks to new-generation LEAP-1A engines, aerodynamic improvements, more sustainable solutions, and lighter materials. The 'United Next' growth plan focuses on up-gauging. It means flying larger narrowbodies on core routes to spread costs across more seats.

Airbus A320ceo vs Boeing 757 vs Airbus A321neo - Comparative Specifications

The A321neo fits perfectly, replacing two older A320s on some frequencies with a single higher-capacity, lower-CASM jet. Over hundreds of rotations per year, this shift produces millions in annual savings. As Simple Flying previously reported, United views the A321neo as its top domestic performer, so replacing an A320 with an A321neo doesn’t just save money.

Indeed, it also creates room for growth without adding more flights into slot-restricted hubs like Newark or San Francisco. In addition, the A321neo LR and especially the XLR variants offer comparable range and capacity to the Boeing 757 but with far greater fuel efficiency. This makes them a wise choice for replacing the 757s on long or thin routes, as seen in the chart above. A similar replacement strategy was adopted by American Airlines as well.

Economics may drive replacement, but passenger experience also significantly influences the choice of replacement. The A321neo arrives factory-fresh with modern interiors, with larger Airspace XL overhead bins, full-color LED mood lighting, fast WiFi, and seat-back entertainment on most configurations. Retrofitting a 1990s-era A320 to this standard is expensive and incomplete; the underlying cabin dimensions and systems limit what can be done.

Passengers notice these differences. On a 2,000-mile domestic leg, the quieter cabin, improved lighting, and better tech of the A321neo create a tangible upgrade over an older A320. Consistency matters too. For example, when a traveler books a premium seat on United, they expect the same product whether they fly from Chicago to Denver or from New York to LA.

By phasing out the A320s, United reduces product variation across its network. For loyalty program members and corporate accounts, this predictability is a selling point. The A321neo becomes a brand ambassador, reinforcing United’s premium domestic positioning while supporting operational efficiency.

The A320 retirement wave is happening alongside a similar story for the 757. Planespotters.net lists 36 757-200s (average age: 29.8 years) and 19 757-300s (average age: 24.3 years) in service at United, with four 757-200s and two 757-300s in storage. According to ch-aviation, the 757-200 is the second-oldest fleet type in United’s mainline operation, behind only the 767-300ER in average age.

This is, in fact, another aircraft to be replaced by newer and bigger jets, such as the 787 Dreamliner. The 757 remains beloved for its performance, especially on 'long and thin' routes, but it is very fuel-hungry compared to new-generation narrowbodies.

The A321neo and XLR close much of the capability gap while offering better per-seat economics and lower emissions. United’s A321neo deliveries will increasingly replace 757 capacity, particularly on transcontinental routes and select shorter transatlantic sectors.

This is a rare dual-fleet transition. United is effectively using the same Airbus type to replace two very different workhorses: the 150 to 170-seat A320 and the 180 to 240-seat 757. For network planning, this simplifies maintenance and training while introducing a modern, flexible airframe into multiple mission profiles.

The decision to accelerate retirements in 2025 was partly economic and partly strategic. Kirby’s comments at the Barclays industrial event in early 2025 made clear that softer leisure demand and macroeconomic headwinds are shaping the near-term fleet plan. Instead of flying marginally profitable old aircraft, United will ground or part out some of the costliest frames, generating a cash-positive effect, per ch-aviation.

Fleet withdrawals will be phased, starting with the oldest A320s. Then, the 757-200s are also likely candidates for the early retirement list, although United has not confirmed specific tail numbers. United has ordered hundreds of Airbus jets, including 50 A321XLRs and 130 A321neos.

United has since outlined a clearer retirement schedule. In October 2025, it said its A319 and A320 fleets would be retired by 2030. In July 2026, it added that it expects to retire around 19 aircraft in 2026 and roughly 80 in 2027 as A321neo deliveries continue and the first 737 MAX 10s enter the fleet. After delays, the A321XLR is set to enter international service on December 1, 2026, flying from Washington Dulles to Amsterdam and Dublin.

United recently took delivery of its 1,000th aircraft, the much-loved Airbus A321neo, but behind the scenes, another aircraft is quietly retiring.

Phasing out the A320s and older 757s is about reshaping the domestic and near-international network. Larger, more efficient narrowbodies let United consolidate frequencies while preserving or even growing total seats. This is vital in congested airports like Newark (EWR) and San Francisco (SFO), where slot constraints limit how many departures an airline can add.

For passengers, the shift will mean a more consistent onboard product, more modern cabins, and fewer operational disruptions caused by aging aircraft. For the airline, it’s a long-term play that supports its carbon-reduction goals, trims fuel burn per seat, and positions United to compete strongly against Delta and American, both of which are also renewing their narrowbody fleets.

Ultimately, the retirement of the Airbus A320ceo fleet is a strategic step toward a more unified, efficient, and passenger-friendly United Airlines. The A321neo, along with the 737 MAX and the 787 Dreamliner for the long-haul, will define the airline’s flying experience well into the 2030s.

In a competitive US market, fleet modernization isn't optional, it’s essential. United’s move away from the older jets toward the A321neo series reflects the industry’s trajectory: efficiency and passenger comfort in one high-capacity package.

#6255. How Many Miles Per Gallon Does An Airbus A380 Get Per Passenger Compared To An A320?

Brandon's passion for aviation started at a young age. He became involved in the flight simulator and VATSIM communities, which sparked his interest in aviation and eventually led him to earn his private pilot license. Outside of work, he continues to build flight hours, explore new airports, and stay involved in the aviation community.

The Airbus A380 burns approximately 4,600 gallons (17,400 L) of fuel per hour. The Airbus A320 burns approximately 750 gallons (3,000 L). Framed as raw fuel consumption, the A380 uses roughly six times as much fuel as the A320, which is not a surprising difference, given that one is a 1,268,000-pound (575,000 kg), four-engine, double-deck widebody and the other is a 172,000-pound (78,000 kg), twin-engine narrowbody. The comparison becomes more interesting when the calculation accounts for how many passengers each aircraft carries per unit of fuel it burns.

Per-passenger fuel efficiency is where the numbers shift, and where factors like seating configuration, load factor, and mission profile start to matter more than total fuel burn. An A380 carrying 615 passengers produces a very different per-passenger figure than one carrying 400 in a premium-heavy layout, and both look different from an A320 flying a two-hour domestic hop versus a four-hour cross-country route.

The Airbus A380 burns approximately 4,600 gallons (17,400 L) per hour during cruise, powered by four Rolls-Royce Trent 900 or Engine Alliance GP7200 engines. At 10 gallons per nautical mile, it consumes more fuel per hour than any other commercial aircraft in service. The A380 carries up to 82,000 gallons (310,000 L) of fuel in its wing and fuselage tanks, enough to sustain flights of up to 8,000 nautical miles (14,800 km) at a cruise speed of Mach 0.85.

The Airbus A320ceo burns approximately 750 gallons (2,840 L) per hour in cruise, powered by two CFM56 or IAE V2500 engines. The A320neo, equipped with CFM LEAP-1A or Pratt & Whitney GTF engines, reduces that figure to approximately 676 gallons (2,560 L) per hour, a 15-20% improvement over the older variant. The A320 carries approximately 6,300 gallons (24,200 L) of fuel, enough for its typical mission profile of 2-4 hour flights covering up to 3,300 nautical miles (6,100 km).

The A380 burns roughly six times as much fuel per hour as an A320. That ratio reflects the difference in aircraft size, engine count, and mission. The A380's maximum takeoff weight is 1,268,000 pounds (575,000 kg). The A320's is approximately 172,000 pounds (78,000 kg). The A380 carries between 400 and 615 passengers depending on configuration. The A320 carries between 150 and 180. The raw fuel burn comparison is not useful on its own without accounting for how many passengers each aircraft carries on the fuel it consumes.

Dividing each aircraft's fuel burn by its passenger count produces a comparison that looks very different from the raw hourly figures. The math is straightforward. The A380 burns approximately 8.2 gallons per statute mile at cruise. In a typical three-class configuration carrying 525 passengers, that works out to roughly 64 passenger-miles per gallon. In Emirates' higher-density 615-seat layout, the figure improves to approximately 75 passenger-miles per gallon.

The A320ceo burns approximately 1.45 gallons per statute mile at cruise. With 170 passengers on board, that produces roughly 117 passenger-miles per gallon. With 180 passengers in a higher-density layout, the figure rises to approximately 124. The A320neo, burning roughly 1.3 gallons per mile, pushes the number higher still, reaching approximately 130-138 passenger-miles per gallon depending on configuration.

The A320 is the more fuel-efficient aircraft per passenger, and by a significant margin. A typical A320ceo delivers roughly 117 passenger miles per gallon compared to approximately 64-75 for the A380. The A320neo widens the gap further. The result may seem counterintuitive given the A380's scale, but the A320 benefits from having only two engines, a lighter airframe relative to its passenger count, and a more modern aerodynamic design in the NEO variant. The A380 spreads its fuel burn across more passengers than any other aircraft in service, but not enough to close the efficiency gap with a modern narrowbody.

The per-passenger figures in the previous section assume every seat is occupied. In practice, no commercial flight operates at 100% load factor. The global average for international flights hovers around 82-85%, and individual flights vary widely depending on route, day of week, time of year, and market conditions. Load factor directly affects the per-passenger efficiency calculation because the aircraft burns the same amount of fuel regardless of how many seats are filled.

An A380 configured with 525 seats at 85% load factor carries approximately 446 passengers. Its per-passenger efficiency drops from 64 passenger-miles per gallon to roughly 54. At a 70% load factor and carrying 368 passengers, the figure falls to approximately 45. Emirates operates its A380 fleet at consistently high load factors, often above 80%, which is part of why the aircraft remains economically viable for the airline. An operator running the same aircraft at a 65% load factor on a less-popular route would see per-passenger fuel efficiency deteriorate to levels that make the economics difficult to justify relative to a smaller widebody.

The A320 follows the same math but starts from a higher baseline. At 85% load factor with 170 seats, the A320ceo carries 145 passengers and delivers roughly 100 passenger-miles per gallon. At 70%, carrying 119 passengers, the figure drops to approximately 82. Configuration matters independently of load factor. An A380 with a premium-heavy cabin carrying 400 passengers at full capacity produces worse per-passenger efficiency than the same aircraft configured with 615 economy seats at 80% load factor.

The A380 and A320 operate on fundamentally different mission profiles, which affects how their fuel efficiency should be interpreted. Every flight includes a takeoff and climb phase that burns significantly more fuel per minute than cruise. On a two-hour A320 domestic flight, the takeoff and climb can account for 20-25% of the total fuel consumed. On a 14-hour A380 long-haul sector, the same phase represents a much smaller percentage of total burn because the aircraft spends the majority of its flight time at cruise altitude where fuel consumption per mile is lowest.

This means the A320's per-passenger efficiency on a short domestic sector is worse than its cruise-phase numbers suggest, while the A380's efficiency on a long-haul flight benefits from spending most of the mission at its most efficient operating point. A 90-minute A320 shuttle flight from New York to Washington burns more fuel per passenger-mile than the same aircraft flying a four-hour cross-country route, simply because the fuel-intensive takeoff and climb phase represents a larger share of the shorter mission.

The two aircraft also serve different economic functions, making a direct efficiency comparison of limited practical value. Airlines do not choose between an A380 and an A320 for the same route. The A380 exists to move 500-plus passengers between major international hubs where demand justifies the capacity. The A320 is designed to carry 150-180 passengers on domestic and short-haul international routes where frequency matters more than size. Comparing their fuel efficiency is useful for understanding how aircraft size, engine count, and mission profile affect per-passenger consumption, but it does not represent a choice any airline actually faces.

Both the A380 and the A320ceo are older-generation aircraft when measured against what is now available. The A350, which Airbus positions as the A380's effective successor on long-haul routes, achieves approximately 100 passenger-miles per gallon in a typical three-class configuration. That represents a roughly 30-50% improvement over the A380, depending on configuration and load factor, achieved through two engines instead of four, extensive composite construction, and Rolls-Royce Trent XWB engines that are a full generation newer than those that power the A380. The Boeing 787 delivers similar per-passenger efficiency gains over the four-engine widebodies it was designed to replace.

The A320neo improves on the A320ceo by 15-20% on a per-seat basis through its LEAP-1A or GTF engines and aerodynamic refinements, including sharklets. At approximately 130-138 passenger-miles per gallon, the A320neo is the most fuel-efficient narrowbody in its class. The A321neo and A321XLR push the family's efficiency further on longer routes where cruise represents a larger share of total fuel burn. The 737 MAX family offers comparable improvements over the 737NG generation.

The generational gap between the A380 and the aircraft replacing it is larger than the gap between the A320ceo and the A320neo. The A380 is being overtaken by aircraft that carry fewer passengers but burn so much less fuel per seat that the total operating economics favor the smaller aircraft on all but the highest-demand routes. The A320ceo is being replaced by a direct successor that does the same job more efficiently on the same routes.

#6254. Report: Lufthansa to Cut 1,000 Jobs

Lufthansa Group plans to lay off around 1,000 full-time workers at its flagship carrier as elevated fuel prices and service disruptions continue to undercut earnings.

The airline group disclosed the cuts in a letter sent to employees and seen by Dow Jones Newswire, according to The Wall Street Journal. The reductions will target Lufthansa’s hubs in Frankfurt and Munich.

Company leaders said their 2024 turnaround plan, initially expected to boost earnings by €2.5 billion over four years, is no longer enough to keep the brand on solid financial ground.

“The year 2026 has set us back: the war in the Middle East, the still very high fuel costs, nine days of strike action, and our already very high cost base have intensified the situation,” the letter said.

Lufthansa failed to reach an agreement with its pilot union earlier this week, setting the stage for a possible work stoppage. The impasse has already resulted in two short strikes, one in February, the other in March.

Lufthansa Group has spoken openly about the damage caused by higher fuel prices over the last nine months. Over the summer, it retired aircraft, cut routes, and warned that layoffs were likely unless prices eased.

According to EuroNews, Lufthansa has lost on average about €20 million per month since the start of the year.

#6253. Why The Airbus A350-1000 Is The Only Jet That Can Fly Sydney To London Nonstop

Qantas is gearing up to launch the world’s longest-ever commercial service between Sydney and London At 9,188 nautical miles (10,573 miles or 17,016 km) and scheduled to exceed 20 hours, the nonstop journey linking the Australian city and English capital will far outdo anything attempted by an airline before. But such an undertaking is no mean feat, and is something that cannot simply be served by any old aircraft.

The Airbus A3350-100ULR (Ultra Long Range) will be used as a result, having been developed specifically for the task. Qantas ordered 12 of these from Airbus in May 2022 under its “Project Sunrise” plan to begin flying direct routes from Sydney Airport (SYD) to both New York John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) and London Heathrow Airport (LHR). Expectations are currently for the first of these to arrive next April, leaving the inaugural record-breaking flight at some point later in the year.

Tweaks have been made to the existing Airbus A3501000 in order to bring the aircraft up to standard for the extreme distance. Though the conventional -1000 is impressive in itself, a 9,000-nautical-mile (10,357-mile or 16,668-km) range leaves its capabilities just shy of those needed for the ambitious connection.

Besides structural improvements and reinforced landing gear to allow for an increased maximum take-off weight (MTOW), an extra rear center tank has been permanently fitted to the -1000ULR. The addition of this tank marks the most significant change between the duo. Able to hold 5,283 (US) gallons (20,000 liters), it takes the -1000ULR’s usable fuel capacity to 48,893 gallons (185,076 liters), according to airport and maintenance planning documents from Airbus.

Select Airbus A350 XWB passenger variant specifications:

Additional fuel capacity, naturally, translates to extended range. In the case of the -1000ULR, the extra tank allows distances of up to 9,800 nautical miles (11,278 miles or 18,150 km) to be flown. It is, by design, perfect for the Sydney and London link thanks to this additional fuel capacity, building on the already strong range boasted by the -1000.

Behind the -1000ULR’s boosted range is not just extra fuel capacity, however. In order to make nonstop flights between London and Sydney a reality, concessions have also been required elsewhere. Namely, Qantas’ -1000ULRs are set to have far fewer seats onboard than other Airbus A350 variants.

Where the -1000 typically carries between 350 and 410 passengers in a three-class configuration, Qantas is poised to operate its -1000ULRs with 238 seats in a four-class layout. The difference is pretty stark, especially when you consider that the -1000 can carry up to a maximum of 480 people if needed.

The key reason for this is weight. The -1000ULR has been designed for endurance, while the -1000 was developed with both range and seating in mind. Singapore Airlines, which currently operates the world’s longest route between the Asian city-state and New York, has made the same trade-off with the Airbus A350-900ULR. Here, the specialized variant carries 161 passengers against the 300 to 350 of its counterpart, the Airbus A350-900.

An exciting milestone as the world's first Airbus A350-1000ULR finally takes shape.

Realistically, reduced capacity is probably not something Qantas executives will be overly worried about. Instead, the carrier should find itself able to charge a premium given both the lower availability of tickets, but more importantly, because of the time that can be shaved off the journey by avoiding a stop.

A good example is Singapore Airlines, which is the sole operator of the -900ULR. With no other nonstop services using ultra-long-haul aircraft available between Singapore and New York, the airline has found itself operating alone at arguably the most premium end of the market. One can opt for the shorter journey time, but it will cost them. In this regard, it is no surprise that Singapore operates its -900ULRs with no basic economy seats.

For Qantas, the goal of linking Australia’s east coast and England’s capital equates to “a new dawn of travel” and the “final frontier of aviation” in its own words. Time will tell if the demand for an uninterrupted connection between the two is really there. But up until now, the hub-and-spoke model appears to have served passengers making the journey pretty well. Indeed, the flight is set to be such an undertaking that Qantas will offer an onboard “wellness zone” to “promote movement” during the near day-long amount of time passengers will spend in the air.

The dominant reason the -1000ULR is the only jet that can make it between Sydney and London without stopping is that Boeing, whether intentionally or not, has not developed its own equivalent. Issues at the US plane maker have been well documented in recent years, most recently in terms of the heavily delayed Boeing 777X program.

But despite being Boeing’s latest addition to its widebody portfolio, even the 777X will not match the -1000, let alone the -1000ULR, on range. Per Boeing, the 777-8 and 777-9 will be able to fly 8,745 nautical miles (10,064 miles or 16,200 km) and 7,285 nautical miles (8,383 miles or 13,500 km) respectively. This means neither will be close to being capable of making the journey that the -1000ULR is designed for. That said, each offers advantages in terms of capacity and payload against the A350 and, in particular, -1000ULR, so the argument is that they have been developed for a different purpose.

This differing design philosophy stretches to the Boeing 787, too. While the Dreamliner made regular nonstop flight between Australia and the United Kingdom possible, the -1000ULR has promised to go a step further. Qantas began flying between Perth and London in 2018 thanks to the 787, but the family's maximum 7,865-nautical-mile (9,050-mile or 14,570-km) range has meant a trip significantly further down under from London has always been out of question.

A key factor the airline can capitalize on is that Qantas will be the only carrier to offer non-stop services on these competitive routes.

As it stands, an unbroken connection between Australia's east and England’s capital remains theoretical. Qantas has planned to start the service for several years, but delays have pushed the inaugural flight further and further back. News of the most recent delay struck earlier this month, placing the first trip somewhere towards the back end of 2027.

According to Qantas, the first of its -1000ULRs was in the paint shop in Toulouse getting made up in the airline’s colors as of late May. Test flights were said to be “just weeks away” at the time, with pilot training also “well underway” at Qantas’ new A350 simulator in Sydney.

In the statement shared with Simple Flying, Qantas added: “Next month we'll announce the first route and timing of our inaugural commercial services [...] When these services take off, passengers will save up to four hours off the journey. Three aircraft are needed to run a daily non-stop service on either route [to New York or London]. While the first aircraft delivery has shifted to April 2027, the next four will follow in quick succession, putting us back on our original schedule by November.”

Airbus’ A350 program was born out of the idea that ultra-long-haul was the next frontier in commercial aviation. The 1000ULR has looked to take this a step further. But, Qantas and Airbus have made a bet with the -1000ULR that passengers will be prepared to sit aboard an aircraft for potentially well over 20 hours at a time. Those who have made the trek from London to Sydney might tell you that the journey feels almost endless currently. Perhaps the roughly four hours of travel time the nonstop service will cut may make all the difference.

Peers will be waiting in the wings to gauge Qantas' success, therefore, and whether the -1000ULR's popularity takes off should be revealed through appetite for the Sydney to London or New York connections. Experience would suggest that a break on what would otherwise almost be a full day aboard an aircraft is a necessity for many. But there too, the experience can largely depend on the fare type and whether one is enjoying the bells and whistles of premium service or is crammed into economy class.

So, would you be keen to make the crossing in one fell swoop aboard a Qantas A350-1000ULR? Or, is the prospect of a 20-plus hour nonstop flight just too awful to bear? Feel free to let us know below.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#6251. Jeffries puts immigration bill high on Democratic priority list

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., holds a news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is signaling Democrats will move quickly on immigration legislation when the party reclaims the House in January, while acknowledging it still has work to do in shaping its healthcare agenda.

Jeffries, who is expected to secure his spot as the next speaker during a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday, identified immigration and health care as among the top priorities for the incoming majority during a Tuesday news conference.

“One of the things that we need to do is to move the Dream and Promise Act for DACA recipients and TPS recipients,” Jeffries said, referring to a Democratic bill introduced last year. “We should actually move that bill immediately.”

The proposal aims to create a path to citizenship for certain Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals recipients and Temporary Protected Status holders. Similar legislation has been a top priority for Democrats in both chambers for more than a decade, with Democrats unable to advance this bill in the House while Republicans have held the majority.

Jeffries also reiterated his calls to rein in Immigration and Customs Enforcement and redirect funding allocated to the agency through Republicans' budget law known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, while expressing a desire for bipartisan cooperation on immigration more broadly.

“We think the border should be safe and strong and secure, and we think our immigration system overall is broken,” Jeffries said. “We need to fix it in a comprehensive way, and certainly, it's our hope that a handful of Republicans will be willing to join us, so we can fix it in a bipartisan way.”

On healthcare, however, Jeffries offered fewer specifics, suggesting Democrats still have decisions to make before taking control of the chamber. Democrats broadly agree on the need to restore subsidies for plans purchased through health insurance markets that expired at the end of 2025. But the question of what additional steps the party should pursue with the goal of expanding coverage and lowering prices is likely to be a major test of Democratic leadership’s ability to find consensus among its robust new majority.

When asked how far Democrats want to lower the Medicare eligibility age, Jeffries responded, “that's all part of an ongoing conversation.”

The New York Democrat outlined several broader healthcare priorities, including reversing Medicaid cuts enacted under President Donald Trump, extending Affordable Care Act tax credits, all of which Democrats have vowed to do over the last year.

“Out of the gate, what we clearly have to do is fix our broken healthcare system in terms of the damage that's been done by Donald Trump and MAGA extremists over the last two years, and that clearly involves reversing the Medicaid cuts and extending the Affordable Care Act tax credits, and beginning to engage in supporting medical research, particularly things like research for pediatric cancer,” Jeffries added.

Democrats established a healthcare working group earlier this Congress, led by Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y. and Terri Sewell, D-Ala., to gather perspectives and develop policy proposals as the party works toward a broader agenda.

Without an announced challenger, Jeffries has expressed confidence that he’ll secure the top Democratic spot in the House, brushing aside questions about incoming members who have said they remain “undecided” ahead of Wednesday’s elections. Jeffries, who was introduced as “Speaker Jeffries” on election night, said last week he was “very confident we’ll get there” and confirmed that the caucus will hold a recorded vote in the contest.

Rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., was nominated for speaker by acclamation ahead of her first election to the position in 2007. But Jeffries’ allies portrayed his decision to go forward with a recorded vote as a show of strength after a group of incoming progressives, many aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America, had floated forcing a recorded vote in the internal leadership race.

Jeffries said Tuesday the approach mirrors the caucus’ 2018 transition from minority to majority, giving members an opportunity to weigh in on who is best positioned to lead based on “track record, experience and vision.”

This report was corrected to reflect Rep. Nancy Pelosi’s status as a current member.

#6248. Senators still see NDAA as chance for online safety legislation

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., delivers his opening statement during the hearing on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

Online safety advocates are looking to the annual defense policy bill for action on legislation to expand accountability for online platforms in cases of child sexual exploitation, as they also introduced legislation to make sure those cases aren’t forced into private arbitration.

Senators and advocates expressed support Tuesday for legislation that would expand the ability of victims of online sexual exploitation to sue social media platforms at a hearing focused on dangers children face on the gaming platform Roblox.

The Senate Judiciary Committee’s panel on Crime and Counterterrorism held the hearing after its Chairman Josh Hawley, R-Mo., and ranking member Richard J. Durbin, D-Ill., introduced a bill Monday that would ban pre-dispute arbitration agreements from affecting cases where a minor was harmed online, including by sexual exploitation.

Hawley and Durbin also worked together on a separate bill to expand eligibility for victims of abuse to bring civil suits against online platforms that intentionally, knowingly or recklessly promoted or facilitated the abuse. It would also include penalties for certain platforms that fail to report child pornography violations on their sites.

That bill is included in a manager’s amendment to the Senate’s fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act bill. Durbin encouraged Congress to pass the NDAA “in the closing days” of the session because “protecting children is an important part of it.”

“I have a few weeks left in my service in the United States Senate,” said Durbin, who is retiring at the end of his term in January. “I’m thinking each day it’s coming to an end, but I want it to come [to an] end the right way.”

The subcommittee has spent much of the 119th Congress focused on harms to children online, including from artificial intelligence chatbots.

Tuesday’s hearing included testimony from survivors and experts on child exploitation on Roblox.

Hawley said that victims are bound by pre-dispute agreements with Roblox to settle claims through private arbitration, rather than in court.

“They slam the courthouse door shut in their faces,” Hawley said. “We’re talking about children now, child victims of sexual exploitation online are denied their day in court by the very company that has exposed them to the content to begin with.”

A spokesperson for Roblox said in a statement that “safety has been central” to the platform since its launch.

“We require age checks for chat, place users under 16 in age-based accounts with protective defaults, and block images and video in chat,” the spokesperson said. “A legal position about arbitration is not a measure of a company’s safety record, and a hearing built around it fails to advance safety.”

Myriam Gilles, a professor of law at Northwestern University, told the panel that a 2022 law that ended forced arbitration agreements for victims of sexual assault has gaps. She said Roblox has argued it does not apply to online actions, just “completed physical assault” and does not apply to platforms.

She also said that Hawley’s new arbitration bill would enhance the effects of his measure regarding civil suits by making sure those suits can be heard publicly if families so choose.

“Congress can pass laws, but if [suits] just get shunted into private arbitration, they’re doing no good in the world,” Gilles said. “A right to sue that ends in secret arbitration is a right in name only.”

The hearing came the same day that advocates, including reality TV personality and activist Paris Hilton, held a press conference to urge House action on a bill (S 1837) that would allow individuals to bring civil suits over nonconsensual intimate depictions generated by artificial intelligence or for possession or production of deepfake porn if there was also intent to disclose the images.

That bill passed the Senate in January but has not been taken up in the House.

When you're traveling for work, a canceled flight is more than a hassle. It can mean missing an important meeting or paying up for a last-minute fare.

Through the end of January 2027, Capital One is giving select business cardholders a new way to manage flight disruptions. Eligible flights booked through Capital One Business Travel will automatically include free rebooking on another airline after a qualifying cancellation or delay, with Capital One covering the new ticket up to $5,000 per traveler.

When travelers book flights through Capital One Business Travel, Capital One will monitor eligible itineraries beginning 24 hours before departure. If the flight is canceled or delayed by at least three hours, the traveler will receive a notification and gain access to a self-service rebooking tool.

The benefit covers several types of disruptions, including:

Last week's ground stop, which backed flights up for days, is a good example of when this benefit could be a huge help.

And unlike traditional airline rebooking, which may be limited to flights operated by the original carrier or its partners, Capital One's tool allows eligible travelers to select a replacement flight on another airline, with the new ticket covered up to $5,000 per traveler.

The flexibility to jump to a competing airline is the standout feature. When one carrier is sold out, another airline may still have space. Re-routing through a different connecting airport can also be strategic to avoid weather issues altogether.

Replacement flights must depart on the same or following day, serve the original destination or a nearby airport and be booked in the same (or lower) fare class. Despite these terms, this will still give travelers far more flexibility than handling things independently.

Travelers can also contact a live agent for 24/7 support.

Capital One Business Travel is available to cardholders with several Capital One business cards, including the following:

Holding one of these cards does not guarantee the free add-on. To check, log in to Capital One Business Travel. If the complimentary rebooking feature is available to you, it will be automatically added to your eligible flight at checkout.

The Venture X Business is particularly relevant for frequent flyers because it earns 5 miles per dollar spent on flights booked through Capital One Business Travel. Plus, it comes with a $300 annual credit for bookings made through Capital One Business Travel.

New applicants can potentially get even more value from Capital One Business Travel through the card's current welcome offer, which includes up to 300,000 bonus miles and a $1,000 travel credit after meeting two spending thresholds:

The information for the Capital One Spark Classic for Business, Capital One Spark Miles for Business, Capital One Spark Miles Select for Business, Capital One Spark Pro and Capital One Spark Classic Miles for Business has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

Related: Capital One Venture X Business review: High earning rates and premium perks for businesses

This is useful protection, but it comes with restrictions. The original ticket must be booked through Capital One Business Travel, and the disruption must meet the three-hour threshold within 24 hours of departure.

It's also temporary. The complimentary is available for eligible bookings made through the end of January 2027, while supplies last. Capital One hasn't published a final eligible departure date.

Still, this could be valuable for business travelers with time-sensitive trips. It can also eliminate business travel bottlenecks, such as waiting for a manager to approve a costly replacement ticket.

Related: Getting a refund for a canceled or delayed flight

Capital One's new feature will help you with rebooking options, but it won't cover the other costs of getting stranded.

For example, if you're rebooked on a flight the following day, you may need to pay for a hotel, meals or transportation. That's where eligible credit card trip delay coverage could help.

Trip delay insurance covers unexpected costs related to qualifying delays, such as accommodations, meals or transportation while waiting out your delay.

That gap can be especially important during weather or air traffic control disruptions, when airlines generally do not pay for stranded travelers' hotels or meals.

Not every eligible card includes trip delay coverage, though. The Venture X Business covers up to $500 per ticket for meals and lodging when a trip is delayed six hours or more or requires an overnight stay.* Cash-back cards like the Spark Cash don't include it. Check your card's benefits guide before you travel.

Related: Flight delayed? 4 things to do to get trip delay reimbursement from your credit card

Capital One's complimentary flight disruption rebooking could be a valuable perk for business travelers facing cancellations or lengthy delays, particularly when another airline can get them to their destination sooner.

And it costs you nothing extra when booking on Capital One Business Travel.

The promotion is available to select Capital One customers for a limited time, so check whether the benefit appears at checkout before relying on it for an upcoming trip.

*For Capital One products listed on this page, some of the benefits may be provided by Visa® or Mastercard® and may vary by product. See the respective Guide to Benefits for details, as terms and exclusions apply.

It's here! Frontier Airlines is now offering its GoWild All You Can Fly Pass for 2027, letting travelers take to the skies at a deep discount for an entire year (and potentially longer).

For a limited time, flyers can purchase a GoWild Pass good through 2027 for just $399. Members of the airline's Discount Den can score the pass for $349.

While that's not quite as good as some offers we've seen in past years (but better than some in other years), it can add up to significant savings if you fly the airline a lot. You must be a Frontier Miles member to purchase one.

Keep in mind that passholders pay $0.01 in airfare plus applicable taxes, fees and charges at the time of booking, so the pass gets you out of the regular airfare, but you're still on the hook for taxes and fees as well as other charges for things like optional seat selection and bags. While taxes on domestic legs are low, international ones can incur $60-$110 each way, depending on the destination.

Sneak peek: Frontier's new first-class seats are finally on sale, set for March debut

Multiple passholders can book travel at the same time, but you can't mix and match passholders with non-passholders on the same reservation.

Likewise, different types of fares can be combined each way on itineraries as long as all passengers hold a valid GoWild Pass at the time of booking and the primary passenger holds a Discount Den membership if Discount Den fares are selected.

One other big caveat: GoWild passes autorenew, so if you want to cancel when your current pass expires, you'll need to contact the airline to do so. Your renewal date will be stated in your confirmation email when purchasing the pass.

The GoWild Pass is valid for flights to over 100 destinations across Frontier's route network, including both domestic gateways and international cities in Mexico, the Caribbean and Central America. The airline's route network changes frequently, though, so stay on top of it to make sure your route will be in service when it's time to book.

Travel begins after purchase (meaning as soon as today) and is available through Dec. 31, 2027, meaning potentially over a full year of flying.

There are no blackout dates, like we've seen in some past instances, but on peak dates, you can expect to pay $59-$199 extra per segment.

Here's the kicker: Standard bookings for eligible GoWild fares begin a day before departure for domestic flights and 10 days before departure for international flights. If your return flight is outside that window, then you'll have to try to make an additional booking when the window opens for that flight.

If you do want to book more in advance than that, however, you can pay an additional charge to do so, though this can vary based on the date and the route.

Also keep in mind that just because a seat is open on the flight you want does not mean it's eligible for a GoWild booking.

You can earn Frontier Miles on the purchase of the pass as well as any extras, like seat assignments, bag fees or priority boarding that you purchase.

If you hold elite status with Frontier, you are still eligible for your benefits, including free seats and bags, so that can be a great way to save on optional fees that non-elites have to pay.

All-you-can-fly airline passes are a rarity these days and come with lots of limitations. Frontier Airlines' GoWild All You Can Fly Pass is no exception.

Still, if you fly the airline a lot, have flexibility (and a bit of spontaneity) in your plans and don't need a ton of extra amenities like preferred seats or checked bags, these fares can be a good way to save a bit on flights you'd be taking anyway ... or perhaps some fun last-minute fares you wouldn't be able to take advantage of otherwise.

#6241. Why You Almost Never See Another Plane From The Window At 35,000 Feet

Brandon's passion for aviation started at a young age. He became involved in the flight simulator and VATSIM communities, which sparked his interest in aviation and eventually led him to earn his private pilot license. Outside of work, he continues to build flight hours, explore new airports, and stay involved in the aviation community.

The assumption behind the question is that aircraft at cruise are spread across enormous distances, and that is not what the regulations require. Between 29,000 (FL290) and 41,000 feet (FL410), the band where most long-haul flights cruise, the minimum vertical separation is 1,000 feet (305 meters). Laterally, radar separation runs to five nautical miles (9.3 km) enroute and three nautical miles (5.6 km) in terminal areas. An aircraft meeting those minimums is close enough to be plainly visible in good conditions.

What keeps most passengers from noticing is the shape of the view, not the distance involved. A cabin window is small, sits at shoulder height, and faces sideways, which rules out the one position where traffic is most likely to be: directly above or below. Aircraft that pass laterally do so quickly, and on a quiet routing there may be nothing within the window’s field of view for hours at a time. In busy corridors, passengers regularly see other aircraft.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) defines RVSM airspace as any airspace between FL290 and FL410 inclusive, where eligible aircraft are separated vertically by 1,000 feet. That band covers almost all long-haul cruise flying, which means the aircraft nearest to a passenger at 35,000 feet (10,668 meters) is frequently one flight level above or below, rather than somewhere over the horizon.

The standard was not always this tight. RVSM reduced the vertical minimum from 2,000 feet (609 meters) to 1,000 feet (305 meters), and the global framework is in ICAO Doc 9574, the manual on implementing a 984-foot (300 meters) vertical separation minimum between FL290 and FL410 inclusive. In the US, the rules appear in 14 CFR 91.706 and Appendix G to Part 91. Above FL410, separation returns to 2,000 feet, which is why the band has a defined upper limit rather than continuing indefinitely.

A thousand feet is close by any ordinary measure. It is roughly three times the length of a Boeing 777-300ER, and an aircraft at that vertical distance passing overhead is larger in the sky rather than a distant speck. Passengers who do catch sight of opposite-direction traffic at cruise often describe it as startlingly close, which is a reasonable reaction to the geometry involved rather than a sign that anything has gone wrong. The separation is deliberate, monitored, and the product of a decades-long safety case. Aircraft operating in RVSM airspace require specific equipment approval and height-keeping performance monitoring, the conditions on which the reduced minimum rests.

Vertical separation is only half of the picture. When radar separates aircraft at the same altitude, the standard minimum is three nautical miles (5.6 km) within 40 nautical miles (74 km) of the antenna and five nautical miles (9.3 km) beyond 40 nautical miles, under FAA Order JO 7110.65. Enroute centers work to 5 nautical miles below FL600. Those minima can be increased or decreased in specific situations, including wake turbulence sequencing on final approach, where larger gaps apply behind heavier aircraft.

Five nautical miles is a meaningful distance on the ground and a modest one at cruise. Two aircraft on reciprocal tracks at typical cruise speeds close that gap in well under a minute, which means lateral traffic is visible briefly rather than persistently. An aircraft crossing ahead of or behind the cabin window enters and leaves the frame quickly enough that a passenger looking down at a screen will miss it entirely.

The standards are not uniform worldwide. ICAO Doc 4444 sets a horizontal separation minimum of 5 nautical miles under certain radar and surveillance conditions, and in non-radar or oceanic environments the figures grow substantially, reaching 10 to 20 nautical miles (19 to 37 km) where controllers rely on position reports rather than continuous surveillance. A flight crossing the North Atlantic on a track system therefore operates with different numbers than the same aircraft would over the continental US, which affects how much traffic is nearby and how predictably it appears. In surveillance airspace with five-nautical-mile spacing, there can be a great deal of traffic within a short distance of any given aircraft.

If the separation standards put traffic within a few thousand feet vertically and a handful of miles laterally, the reason passengers rarely see anything has to lie elsewhere. It lies where a cabin window is and which direction it faces.

A passenger window sits at roughly shoulder height along the side of the fuselage, which produces a field of view that extends sideways and downward. It does not extend upward in any useful way, and it does not extend forward or aft beyond a narrow arc. Traffic 1,000 feet directly above the aircraft, which under RVSM is the single most likely position for another aircraft to occupy, is in the one place a seated passenger cannot look. Traffic 1,000 feet directly below is slightly better placed but still largely obscured by the wing on most seats.

That leaves lateral traffic, which is visible but brief. An aircraft five miles away at a similar altitude occupies a small part of the sky, and at combined closing speeds approaching 1,000 knots on reciprocal headings, it moves through the available arc quickly. Looking out of a window at the right moment is a matter of timing rather than frequency.

Conditions compound it. Cloud layers above or below the cruise altitude hide traffic entirely. Haze reduces contrast at distance. In daylight, an aircraft against a bright sky is harder to pick out than the same aircraft against darkness at night, when navigation and anti-collision lights make it considerably more obvious. Most of the reports from passengers who have clearly seen nearby traffic at cruise come from night flights, where there is something lit to see.

The current standard is relatively recent. The North Atlantic became the first ICAO region to implement the reduced vertical separation minimum on March 27, 1997, applying it initially at flight levels 330 through 370. The entire Western Hemisphere implemented RVSM across FL290 to FL410 on January 20, 2005, and Africa followed on September 25, 2008. The rollout therefore took just over a decade from the first region to the last.

Halving the vertical minimum roughly doubled the number of usable cruise levels in the band. At 2,000-foot spacing, FL290 through FL410 offers seven levels. At 1,000-foot spacing, it offers thirteen, which is the capacity argument that drove the change. The FAA describes RVSM as allowing aircraft to fly more optimal profiles, save fuel, and increase airspace capacity; a Federal Register notice on the rule stated that RVSM saves fuel and minimizes traffic delays by accommodating more aircraft on the most fuel-efficient routes available.

The efficiency gain comes from altitude rather than distance. An aircraft burns less fuel at the altitude its weight and the conditions favor, and that altitude changes during a flight as fuel burns off. Before RVSM, a crew wanting to climb had to wait for a level 2,000 feet higher to be free. With 1,000-foot spacing, the next available level is closer to the one the aircraft is already at, making step climbs easier to obtain and keeping more aircraft nearer their optimum profile.

The safety case required equipment and monitoring to match. Aircraft operating in RVSM airspace need specific approval, and height-keeping performance is monitored on an ongoing basis.

Elevating or descending? Cruising altitude is a direct result of safety, fuel use, and comfort in a myriad of ways.

Framing this as something passengers almost never see overstates it. In busy airspace, other aircraft are visible regularly, and anyone who flies often enough will have seen traffic passing above or below on a clear day.

The places to look are the places where aircraft concentrate. Oceanic track systems funnel traffic onto a small number of parallel routes at similar altitudes, which is why passengers crossing the North Atlantic frequently see other aircraft on adjacent tracks or one level away. The same applies to major continental corridors, where traffic converges on the same waypoints regardless of origin and destination. Terminal areas produce the most sightings of all, with separation reduced to 3 nautical miles and aircraft at a range of altitudes during climb and descent rather than spread across a single cruise band.

Night flying improves the odds considerably. Anti-collision strobes and navigation lights are visible at distances where the airframe itself would be invisible in daylight, and the contrast against a dark sky does the rest. Passengers on overnight transatlantic and transpacific flights report seeing other aircraft more often than those on daytime sectors, which reflects visibility rather than traffic density.

The flight deck sees more than the cabin does, which is the clearest indication that the aircraft are there. A forward-facing windscreen covers the arc where converging and opposite-direction traffic appears, and crews receive traffic information from controllers and from TCAS regardless of what is visible. For passengers, the view is sideways, the window is small, and the aircraft most likely to be nearby is in the one direction the window does not cover.

#6239. Hill GOP looking to trim White House's $50 billion aviation ask

Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy conducts a news conference on the recent nationwide ground stop after meeting with Senate Republicans in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Senate Republicans poured cold water Tuesday on the administration’s new ask for a $50.1 billion emergency air traffic control and airport infrastructure package, arguing much of it has little to do with the immediate problems that led to a nationwide ground stop on Friday.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought last week asked for $30.1 billion before Duffy voiced support for the rest of the funds at a Friday night press conference on the ground stop.

The original ask contained roughly $12 billion that was tied directly to air traffic control upgrades, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said, with the remainder going toward long-sought airport terminal and other upgrades to aging aviation facilities.

Duffy and Vought laid out in a letter to House and Senate appropriators on Tuesday what the extra $20 billion would be for — half for construction of five new air route traffic control centers, and half for construction, replacement and improvement of up to 140 air traffic control towers.

They justified the increased demand because of the “urgent need” that became evident after the ground stop. Duffy and Federal Aviation Administrator Bryan Bedford fanned out across the Capitol to try to sell the request, including a stop at Senate Republicans’ weekly policy lunch.

But it quickly became evident that their own allies on Capitol Hill want more and better justification for why so much extra money is needed.

Not only are there concerns that much of the request would go to terminal reconstruction and other longer-term projects, but lawmakers keep noting the FAA hasn’t yet spent about $8 billion out of the initial $12.5 billion “down payment” on air traffic control modernization provided in last year’s budget reconciliation law.

“I don’t think the full $50 billion will be funded,” Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, said Tuesday. “What we just discussed there, and what I expressed, is that the request needs to be focused on safety modernization.”

Still, Cruz said the administration had done a “good job” with the initial $12.5 billion modernization plan so far and he expected to see continued bipartisan support for the effort.

Senate Republicans are considering adding additional aviation funds through a filibuster-proof reconciliation bill, a process that could begin as soon as this week with a floor “vote-a-rama” on a resolution to unlock that process. Cruz said that while reconciliation could be the vehicle used, additional aviation funds need to be “safety-focused.”

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., said after the lunch with Duffy and Bedford that he expects Congress will look at a package more in the $10 billion to $30 billion range.

For his part, Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., said the airline industry itself should foot at least a portion of the bill, considering how much federal support the carriers have received over the years.

“I don't understand why the airline industry doesn't pay for it. We give them unbelievable amounts of money,” Scott said, adding that he doesn’t like adding to the deficit and is “not big on government running things.”

Duffy explained the need for the high price tag as the result of decades of pent-up demand that are now threatening major disruptions and safety risks to the traveling public.

“This has never been done. To be clear, we are keeping planes safe in the sky, and we are switching out equipment that’s been a problem for decades,” he said. “I and the president have decided we are going to lean in and fix it.”

He called the effort a “historic investment” reflecting the ways air travel has changed since much of the nation’s infrastructure was built — noting that the newest tower was constructed in 1969 and much of the software being used is from the 1990s. Still, Duffy said, on the current course of funding, it would take 300 years to replace every U.S. tower.

“I'm not going to tell [Congress] how to do their work, but I'm telling everybody what we need,” Duffy said. “And whether it's a party-line vote or if it's a bipartisan vote, I do think this is one moment in a very charged political environment — one moment where almost all Americans and bipartisan members of both bodies are kind of in agreement that we should lean in to do this.”

Even as Duffy petitioned for additional funds Tuesday, he said that the “root cause” of the equipment instability that made the ground stop necessary is still unclear as investigators analyze the router that caused the problem.

A “routine switchover” from old copper wires to digital fiber in the telecommunications system “started to create issues in our network,” Duffy explained Tuesday.

The telecommunications transition includes the conversion of thousands of routers to what are known as Juniper devices — a process being undertaken by contractor L3Harris Technologies. Duffy and Bedford explained that 68 other routers had been converted without incident prior to the problematic switchover Friday.

Bedford said Tuesday that use of the router that officials have identified as the source of the system instability has been suspended “and we've disabled the ones that are out there.”

The decision to suspend use of the router followed an inquiry sent to the agency by Senate Commerce Committee Democrats a day prior. “With thousands of conversions remaining, FAA must address outstanding safety and reliability concerns before expanding installation,” they wrote.

Bedford said he was “highly confident” that similar problems wouldn’t erupt again. “Every element of this is going to be analyzed to see what we learn here and make sure that it doesn't get repeated,” he said.

David Jordan, Lia Chien and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

#6236. Jet2 Launches 18 New Routes In Only 4 Weeks: See All Flights Now

Jet2 is the fourth-largest airline serving the UK by flights and seats for sale this year. Formally called Jet2.com, the leisure operator has 14 bases across the country, with London Gatwick being the most recent addition back in March 2025.

Ch-aviation shows that Jet2 currently has 134 aircraft. Excluded are the Airbus A330-200s that were leased from AirTanker, which provided additional capacity, mainly for the peak season, for nine years. The agreement has now ended.

Obviously, most of Jet2's activity revolves around the summer, which has the highest demand. In August 2026, for example, the leisure airline had 3.2 million round-trip seats for sale. That's the top month, which revolves around school holidays. In contrast, Jet2's capacity was reduced to 1.3 million seats in November and slightly less again in December. Despite this, multiple new routes are starting, with November's additions shown below.

The focus in the winter necessarily changes from fun-in-the-sun trips to skiing and trips to visit Christmas markets. All but one of the following additions are for markets. The exception is Agadir, which is relatively warm in the winter and is geared to that. Of course, the huge shift from summer to winter operations is absolutely nothing unusual. In the past, charter and other leisure airlines used the much quieter winter to perform more in-depth maintenance ahead of the following summer, when utilization grew substantially.

Up to four weekly A321neo (the airline's shortest route this winter)

Strasbourg is a brand-new destination for Jet2. Nicknamed the 'Capital of Christmas,' the French city's oldest festive market supposedly dates back as early as the 1500s. It is reportedly also the oldest version in France. At 348 nautical miles (644 km) each way, Strasbourg will be Jet2's shortest-ever international route from Stansted.

Unsurprisingly, the following additions do not revolve around city breaks for festive shopping but instead skiing and other winter pursuits. This assumes the snow is there in the right quantity and quality. That is not always the case, especially nowadays. All the classic destinations and gateways are served.

All five routes from Gatwick, which is the UK's second-busiest airport, are new to Jet2's network. However, the sole remaining link (Stansted to the Austrian city of Innsbruck) is not new, but it has not been served for a while.

The carrier operated between Stansted and Innsbruck from February 2020 to 2024, so the return comes after nearly three years. What is notable is that flights previously operated until springtime. Nowadays, the season finishes much earlier, which is designed to help ensure more snow.

The ultra-low-cost carrier has no flights on Christmas Day, but things aren't quite as they seem. Find out more here!

As mentioned earlier, Jet2's peak month is August, with 3.2 million seats in 2026. Capacity in November is 59% lower, at 1.3 million seats this year. But it is not the nadir month — January is. That winter month has 902,000 seats in 2026, but, funnily enough, will be lower in 2027.

Let's stick to August and November and compare the capacity gap for Jet2's 14 UK bases: Belfast International, Birmingham, Bournemouth, Bristol, East Midlands, Edinburgh, Gatwick, Glasgow, Leeds/Bradford, Liverpool, Luton, Manchester, Stansted, and Newcastle. Compared to the busiest month, Stansted has the biggest drop in November (seats down 74%). In contrast, Newcastle has the smallest drop (-42%, well below the average of 59%).

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

Jet2 has clearly spotted an opportunity to expand while demand for holidays remains strong.

What better way to kick off the holiday season than by planning your next vacation?

Whether you’re looking to bask in the sun on a tropical Caribbean getaway or explore glaciers along Alaska’s mesmerizing coastline, Norwegian Cruise Line is offering a noteworthy Black Friday deal you don’t want to miss.

NCL is offering 50% off all sailings* — nearly 350 destinations — regardless of itinerary or ship. This lucrative cruise deal lets families, couples or even solo travelers make their dream vacation plans a reality and map out an itinerary well within their budget.

In addition to this Black Friday promotional discount, guests can enjoy an unlimited open bar, shore excursion credits and much more.

Keep reading to find out how you can save money and get more than $2,000 in value on your next cruise booking with this Black Friday deal.

NCL’s 50% off Black Friday deal* applies to all cruises and is available to book for sailings through 2028. To browse sailings for this promotion, visit NCL.com and filter by destination, port of departure, ship and duration to narrow down your perfect itinerary.

Plus, as an added bonus, this promotion can be combined with NCL’s “Free at Sea” package. Delivering more than $2,000 in value, guests can enjoy benefits such as an unlimited open bar, specialty dining, shore excursion credits and Wi-Fi.

This all-inclusive package is great for guests who want to take advantage of key cruise perks without paying a la carte for additional benefits.

And, as if this Black Friday deal couldn’t get any better, on select sailings, kids sail for free. This is a great perk for families looking to travel at a greater cost-saving value.

Note that fare prices shown are in U.S. dollars on a per-person basis and include taxes, fees and port expenses.

With nearly 350 destinations to choose from, including sailings to the Bahamas, Alaska, Europe and the Caribbean, there is no shortage of adventures and options to choose from.

For instance, you could book a four-day getaway to the Bahamas, departing from Orlando, Florida (Port Canaveral) and stopping at Nassau and NCL’s private island, Great Stirrup Cay.

The Bahamian oasis is now home to a 6-acre private water park that features 19 waterslides, cliff jumps, a lazy river and more. Great Tides Waterpark opened in September 2026 and gives guests flexibility to choose their own adventure.

If a full day of thrills isn’t for you, guests can also opt to relax and enjoy the Great Life Lagoon, a 28,000-square-foot pool. For families or couples looking for a quick vacation, this could be the perfect option.

For those wanting to explore several European countries — without the hassle and additional out-of-pocket cost of booking trains, flights or hotel rooms — guests can embark on a nine-day Eurotrip starting from London and cruising to ports in France, Germany, Belgium and Denmark.

This can be a nice option for couples, those traveling with friends or even families.

As a mom of a two-year-old, it can be challenging (and stressful) to navigate trekking across Europe with a toddler. I like that cruising takes the guesswork off of meal plans, nap times and travel between countries.

Plus, unlike other cruise lines, Norwegian is known for its "freestyle cruising," which means there are no enforced dress codes or assigned dining times. As a toddler mom, I like that NCL gives guests the flexibility to book the vacation they want.

Related: The 5 best destinations you can visit on a Norwegian Cruise Line ship

If cruising on a megaship is not your style, NCL offers a resort-like ship class known as the Prima Class. These smaller, more upscale ships feature a more modern aesthetic, larger outdoor areas and elevated experiences.

In March, NCL's newest ship, Norwegian Luna, set sail to destinations in the Caribbean, the Bahamas and Bermuda. This ship has signature Prima Class touches, such as Indulge Food Hall and Cagney's Steakhouse, as well as some must-try additions, including the authentic Thai restaurant Sukhothai.

Standout ship attractions include the Aqua Slidecoaster, the world's first hybrid waterslide and roller coaster, waterfront infinity pools, kids' splash pad, adults-only pool area, game room, and so much more.

Basically, the new Norwegian Luna will make it hard for guests to decide to even leave the ship.

If exploring destinations and being one of the first to set sail on a new ship is enticing, NCL is also extending this promotion to its recently unveiled ship, Norwegian Aura. The biggest ship in Norwegian's fleet will set sail in April 2027 and will feature more expansive spaces, waterslides and attractions around every corner. Itineraries for this ship include ports in the Caribbean, Greek isles, Italy and Spain.

With this 50% off Black Friday deal*, now is a great time to book your 2027 or even your 2028 travel plans and experience these brand-new cruise ships.

Whether you're planning to take advantage of this Black Friday deal or book an NCL cruise, be sure to check out the company's Latitudes Rewards program. This loyalty program is free to join and lets cruisers earn rewards and get access to exclusive discounts, onboard experiences and more.

Members can earn 1 point for every cruise night, and 1 additional point per night for reserving select rooms or when booking with a Latitudes Rewards insider offer.

As you reach a certain threshold of points, you can unlock new status tiers, which may include specialty offers, cabin upgrades, dining benefits and more.

Related: Norwegian Cruise Line’s Latitudes Rewards loyalty program guide

NCL is an award-winning cruise line that offers itineraries for all types of travelers, giving action-packed thrill-seekers or guests seeking a relaxing, elevated sailing experience the flexibility to book a cruise that matches their vacation aesthetic.

And if you want to save (possibly thousands of dollars) on your 2027 or 2028 travel plans, now is the time to book with NCL and receive 50% off all cruises*.

#6234. Is There Still Hope for Postliberalism?

The rejections of Viktor Orbán and Donald Trump hold sobering lessons for the nationalist right.

Former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán (left) and President Donald Trump.

NR Illustration; Marton Monus, Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters

On Election Night this past May in Budapest, I was in the ballroom when a defining political era ended faster than it takes to place a drink order at a party-district ruin bar on a Saturday night. Viktor Orbán, the four-term prime minister who for 16 years was the undisputed sovereign of Hungarian politics, and the monster that haunted the nightmares of globalists from Brussels to Washington, took the stage not long after election results began rolling in — and gracefully accepted defeat. It was as if magician David Copperfield had made the Matterhorn disappear before the audience settled into its chairs on the chalet lawn.

Just like that, Orbán was gone. When I first arrived in Budapest for a fellowship in 2021, a Hungarian conservative friend told me that everybody knows Orbán’s Fidesz Party is riddled with corruption, but people tolerate it because life has been getting better and better for them since the reformist prime minister took power in 2010. “But if the economy ever turns,” he said, “then corruption is going to matter. A lot.”

Former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán (left) and President Donald Trump.

NR Illustration; Marton Monus, Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters

Rod Dreher is the author of six books, including the New York Times bestsellers The Benedict Option (2017) and Live Not By Lies (2020).
