#6232. Senate Dems dismiss talk of earlier leadership election; Schumer confident

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., leaves the Senate Democrats’ lunch meeting in the Capitol on Nov. 10. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Senate Democrats moved Tuesday to squelch talk of an accelerated timeline for the vote for a new majority leader, signaling they intend to keep the contest on Dec. 1.

That the timing of the vote was already becoming a flashpoint in the caucus speaks to the rocky start for the incoming majority despite a near-sweep of key midterm races that could give Democrats 56 seats in the chamber.

The prospect of an earlier vote had been floated as a way to prevent internal divisions from hobbling the incoming majority before the 120th Congress even began.

But supporters of Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., both in the chamber and among party activists outside it, were increasingly casting the idea of a shorter contest as a bid to halt momentum for his bid against Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y.

Even as Schumer maintained that he has the votes necessary to be elected as majority leader, several senators insisted Tuesday the discussion taking place within the caucus was a good thing.

“I’m confident I’ll be the next leader. I have the votes,” Schumer told reporters on Tuesday following the conference’s lunch.

Van Hollen for his part told reporters Tuesday he believes his bid has “momentum at this point in time, which is why there was an effort to short-circuit the process.”

“And fortunately, I think that will fail.”

Several senators leaving the meeting said the topic of the leadership contest did not come up at all, and that neither Van Hollen nor Schumer gave a presentation regarding their bids.

That was in large part due to the absence of the incoming senators — which could be as high as 13, depending on how the dust settles in Alaska — who are able to vote in the leadership elections. Retiring senators do not cast a ballot.

With such a large class of incoming freshman, several incumbents saw it crucial to keep the election scheduled as is.

“No one has ever raised that with me. I mean, I saw a rumor that some were wanting to contemplate that,” Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., said Tuesday after the meeting. “The leadership discussions did not come up today. And part of the reason is we didn’t have the newcomers.”

“Remember, they all get a vote in the leadership discussion, and it would be hard to get them here,” Kaine continued, noting that only Sen.-elect Scott Colom, D-Miss., was present for Tuesday’s lunch amid his belated orientation. “But nobody else was here, and that discussion needs to have the newcomers because newcomers get votes. The outgoers don’t, right?”

Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M. echoed that sentiment on Monday evening, saying, “I want to hear from the freshman class as well.”

Sen. Mazie K. Hirono, D-Hawaii, said, “I don’t know that” when asked about moving up the elections. “I think that we need to make sure that there’s enough time for what I would call a robust discussion about what we’re going to do. I think we should be very embracing of the new people who have been through fire to get here, and I think that we have to make sure that all these voices are heard.

“They’ve got a lot of talent to bring to the table,” she said.

Several senators-elect are among those who have publicly thrown their hats into Van Hollen’s corner, including Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota and Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan.El-Sayed on Tuesday said at The Atlantic Summit that he sees Van Hollen as “unique” in his experience in the Senate and running the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee as well as what he called “a willingness to take risks.”

“We need people who are willing to take legislative risk,” he said. “We need to rethink the way we legislate. It just should not be the process where you make one or two omnibus pieces of legislation that nobody really knows what’s in them,” he continued, advocating for piecemeal legislation.

But there are about 15 Democrats who have publicly backed Schumer’s bid. If former Rep. Mary Peltola maintains her lead in the lone outstanding Senate race in Alaska, Schumer would need 29 to secure the helm of the ship.

“I committed to Sen. Schumer literally months ago, and I continue to support him,” Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., said Monday. “I’m incredibly excited about the new ideas that our new colleagues have, and their energy, and the potential for changing the way we operate in the Senate, which we have to do because we need to be more effective.”

Several incumbents have also thrown their support behind Van Hollen for leadership change, including Sens. Jeff Merkley of Oregon and Bernie Sanders of Vermont.“I think, as I’ve said many times, the American people want change in the way we do business here in Washington, and I think Chris Van Hollen would be a great leader of the Democrats,” Sanders said Monday.

Several senators and senators-elect are refusing to comment publicly on who they’ll back.

That included Sen. Ben Ray Lujan, D-N.M., who said he wants “to hear the commitments from folks that are pursuing this leadership role as well as every leadership position in the Senate, as well as chairs of committees, to what their commitments are to having a strong agenda that’s going to improve people’s lives.”

Kaine is also in that camp, and insisted Monday he hadn’t made up his mind. But he did speak positively of Schumer’s recruiting efforts in the midterms and history of dealing with a Trump White House.

“Schumer just delivered a major win for us. No one who was not on the ballot worked harder for this victory than Chuck Schumer,” he said. “Chuck Schumer also happens to know Donald Trump better than anybody else in the caucus, and dealing with this wounded president is going to be a challenge over the next few years.”

“The voters are also overwhelmingly demanding change,” he said. “So we got to figure that out as a caucus, and we’re going to be able to. And we’re not afraid to have a discussion because we’re Democrats. We like democracy.”

Sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., also remained mum on who he’ll support but said, “You can’t argue” Schumer brought Democrats the majority.

“I think it’s a healthy thing to try and improve how the conference goes about its business,” he said. “I don’t think that is a distraction. We can deal with some distractions. We have to keep our eye on the ball.”

Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., who last week called for new leadership in a news conference with Sanders, days before Van Hollen’s announcement, was noncommittal arriving to the Capitol on Monday if that meant she’d be supporting the Maryland Democrat.

Senate Democrats’ election will most likely be a secret ballot. And most senators remained unified against moving the leadership elections before they recess for the Thanksgiving break.

“They should not be moved up. There was a reason that those rule changes took place before, and they should take place in December,” Lujan said.

Kaine dismissed Van Hollen’s challenge as anything unusual.

“We’re Democrats. It’s frankly unusual that there usually [aren’t] challenges to Democratic leaders because we’re Democrats,” he said. “It’s been a little unusual to have been here for 13 years and not really have them like this. But I think it’s a discussion not just about the two contenders for the leader role, but also the leadership team and priorities, and it’s all wrapped up in one discussion.”

“That’s why we decided, don’t do these votes until December, because you want to let the election settle and understand exactly what’s up, and then hear from potential votes.”

Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., said, “I think we should stick with the rules when it comes to the caucus. … That’s going to be what makes sure that we show that we have a real process.”

Sanders asked: “Why would anyone want to do that?” when asked.

“I think there’s a date that’s been called, and that should be the date.”

Here at TPG, we've used points and miles to reach dream destinations, cover last-minute travel plans and make it easier to visit friends and family.

Here's how your holiday expenses can help you unlock great travel opportunities.

Rewards credit cards almost always extend a welcome offer to new cardholders. These welcome offers are the best and easiest way to earn a huge stash of points or miles. Most cards require that you meet a certain spend threshold in order to earn the welcome bonus.

Your holiday spending can cover a large portion of a card's spending requirement or even get you to the finish line. Some great welcome offers that you might be able to earn with the help of end-of-year purchases include:

Just make sure you're sticking to your existing budget rather than spending extra solely to earn a bonus.

One of my favorite things about points and miles is that their value fluctuates depending on what you redeem them for. If you want to hunt for extremely high-value redemptions that are impossible to afford with just cash, you can.

Or, if you'd rather use your rewards for simple redemptions that get you where you want or need to be, that works, too.

In order to maximize the value of your points and miles, we recommend transferring them to your card's airline and hotel transfer partners. When it's time to head to the grocery store for Christmas dinner or to open your wallet for holiday gifts, you want to have the right card in hand to pay with. Rewards cards generally come with bonus categories that earn multiple points or miles per dollar spent.

For example, a card that earns elevated rewards at grocery stores could be especially useful when shopping for holiday meals, while a card with an online shopping bonus category could help you earn more on gifts.

Through Dec. 31, you can earn 5 points per dollar spent (or 5% cash back) at grocery stores with the , on up to $1,500 in spending (activation required). That makes this card a great choice for your holiday grocery purchases.

If you strategically plan your holiday shopping to max out that $1,500 in spending, you'd earn 7,500 bonus Chase Ultimate Rewards points, which is worth about $154, according to our November 2026 valuations. The Freedom Flex is a favorite card of mine because of how powerful its quarterly categories can be.

If you're shopping with a merchant that isn't covered by any of your cards' bonus categories, use a card that earns more than 1 point or mile per dollar spent on general purchases.

A couple of great examples include the and the Capital One Venture Rewards. The Freedom Unlimited earns 1.5 points per dollar spent on all nonbonus spending, while the Venture Rewards earns 2 miles per dollar spent on all purchases.

Before checking out, it's worth seeing whether your credit card issuer has an offer for the retailer you're shopping with.

Issuers such as American Express, Chase and Capital One extend offers to existing cardholders. These offers generally give cardholders the opportunity to earn bonus cash back, points or miles in exchange for spending with a specific merchant.

During the holiday season, it's important to check your card often for these opportunities. Offers can vary per card, and some issuers may target a cardholder with a specific offer, so you should always monitor them yourself.

These offers can be combined with deals from shopping portals like Rakuten and Rove. A few years ago I purchased a new LG TV during Black Friday through Rakuten. That purchase earned me an additional 30,000 Membership Rewards points, showing just how valuable a well-timed shopping portal promotion can be. That's enough points to cover round-trip economy flights within the U.S.

If you don't hold an eligible Amex card, you can also now earn Bilt Points through Rakuten.

Aside from Rakuten, individual card issuers and airlines also offer online shopping portals that can help you earn your preferred rewards. Overall, if you have any holiday purchases to make, you could be leaving a huge chunk of rewards on the table by skipping out on issuer offers and shopping portals.

Holiday shopping can be a great opportunity to start earning points and miles balance or work on your stash.

By combining rewards credit cards, eligible issuer offers and shopping portals, you could earn valuable rewards to put toward travel in 2027 and beyond. Just make sure you're spending within your budget and paying your credit card balance in full to avoid interest charges that could outweigh the rewards you earn.

With a little work, you can take these kinds of trips without breaking the bank, too.

#6229. Mary Peltola unseats Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska

Former Alaska Rep. Mary Peltola speaks during her election night party in Anchorage on Nov. 3. (Charly Triballeau/ AFP via Getty Images)

Former Rep. Mary Peltola has defeated Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, giving Senate Democrats their ninth pickup of the midterm elections and bringing their caucus’s total seats in the next Congress to 56.

The Associated Press called the race for Peltola around 10:19 p.m. Eastern time on Tuesday, a full two weeks after Election Day. The latest tranche of ballots counted put the former congresswoman past the 50-percent threshold to win the election outright without Alaska’s ranked choice voting system kicking in.

With her victory, Peltola, who is Yup’ik, becomes one of the first Native American women elected to the Senate, along with fellow Democrat Peggy Flanagan, who won the open seat in Minnesota this month.

“As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans’ support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first.,” Peltola said in a statement after the race was called.

The Alaska race was the final Senate contest to be called in a midterm election that saw Democrats win commanding majorities in both chambers of Congress. Besides Alaska, Democrats also flipped Senate seats in North Carolina, Maine, Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Kansas, South Carolina and Mississippi.

Peltola, a former state legislator, made history in 2022 when she became the first Alaska Native elected to Congress, winning a special election for the state’s at-large district. She comfortably won the general election that fall but was narrowly unseated in 2024 by Republican Nick Begich.

She entered the Senate contest in January, positioning herself as an independent-minded Democrat and invoking the legacies of two well-liked Alaska Republicans, the late Sen. Ted Stevens and the late Rep. Don Young, whom she succeeded in the House.

She campaigned on the slogan “fish, family, freedom” and played up her moderate views and deep roots in the state.

But the race was marked by allegations of political gamesmanship. In addition to the incumbent Sullivan, a retired colonel in the U.S. Marine Corps Reserves, the Senate ballot also included a retired teacher named Dan J. Sullivan. The New York Times reported late last month that operatives aligned with Peltola’s campaign were involved in the effort to recruit the second Dan Sullivan in an attempt to confuse voters.

Peltola has said she had no connection to the scheme.

Prior to Election Day, the Trump administration filed a lawsuit seeking to delay certification of the result if Sen. Sullivan were to lose. The lawsuit was tossed earlier this month by a federal judge.

Trump also suggested that all votes cast for Dan J. Sullivan should be added to the incumbent’s total. “If you add them up, Dan Sullivan wins,” the president told reporters Monday. But as of Tuesday evening when the race was called, Peltola had more votes than both Sullivans combined.

The Alaska race was initially viewed as a long shot for Democrats. The Last Frontier has elected a Democratic senator just once in the past 50 years – in 2008, when Mark Begich ousted Stevens. Begich, the Democratic uncle of the current Republican congressman, served a single term before he was ousted by Sullivan in 2014.

But anger in Alaska over the rising cost of food and fuel — already among the highest in the nation — provided Democrats with an opening.

"56 seats was an unimaginable result even just a few months ago," Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer said in a statement Tuesday night. "But I knew if we concentrated on getting the best candidates, and if we focused like a laser on the costs, corruption, and chaos that Donald Trump has wrought throughout America, we would have shot."

In other Alaska races, Democrats flipped the governor’s mansion, with former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins winning an open-seat race to become the first Democrat elected governor of the state since Tony Knowles won a second term in 1998.

The race for the state’s at-large House district will be decided by ranked choice voting, with tabulations expected to take place Wednesday. Begich, the GOP incumbent, was leading Tuesday with 47.5 percent of the vote and is expected to prevail over independent Bill Hill, who had the backing of national Democrats and trailed with 42 percent. Another Democrat and a Libertarian combined for the remainder of the vote.

#6227. Trump Should Press Xi for Joshua Wong’s Release

The democracy activist’s sentence for meeting with American lawmakers ought to be treated as an affront to the U.S.

Pro-democracy activists Joshua Wong and Agnes Chow arrive at the Eastern Court by police van after being arrested on suspicion for organizing illegal protests, in Hong Kong, China, August 30, 2019.

When President Donald Trump meets Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen this Thursday, the agenda will be crowded with tariffs, chips, Taiwan, and the war in Iran. One more item should be on it: Joshua Wong, a 30-year-old Hong Kong democracy activist who was sentenced to ten years in prison for the “crime” of talking to Congress.

On September 2, Wong pleaded guilty in Hong Kong’s High Court to “conspiring to collude with foreign forces,” a crime under Beijing’s notorious National Security Law. As prosecutors laid out their case, they cited Wong’s prior meetings with sitting U.S. lawmakers, including then–Senator Marco Rubio, along with testimony he previously gave to the Congressional-Executive Commission on China. On November 5, Wong was sentenced to ten years in prison.

Benedict Rogers is a human rights activist and writer. He is the senior director at Fortify Rights, the co-founder and chair of Hong Kong Watch, and the author of The China Nexus: Thirty Years In and Around the Chinese Communist Party’s Tyranny.

#6226. 3 Jumbo Jets, 1 President: Every Air Force One Boeing 747 Flies To Asia For Trump’s Trip

Yesterday, US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin met for a trilateral summit in Shenzhen, China. In addition to this unprecedented summit, often referred to as the second Yalta, the meeting is also notable because the United States flew all three Air Force One aircraft to China to accommodate Trump and his entourage.

Trump initially landed in China on November 18, using the Boeing 747-8 that he controversially received as a gift to the American government, alongside the older Boeing 747-200. The other Air Force One 747-200 was also seen in Asia.

It was in Manila, not China, where the presidential fleet made a stopover, that the three Air Force One jumbo jets were spotted together. The 747-8 is by far the newest and bears a white, red, and blue livery that Trump has demanded for presidential aircraft. It is called VC-25B Bridge. The two older jets are painted in the simpler blue-and-white livery, which has been traditional for presidential aircraft. These aircraft are designated VC-25A and have the registration numbers 82-8000 and 92-9000.

The sight of the two jets in Shenzhen was to be expected, as a second Air Force One often accompanies the jet that the president is actually traveling on. It serves as a backup in case mechanical issues strike. However, it is strange that all three aircraft were flying together at least as far as Manila. It is not known for certain whether the third jet also made its way to China or was employed on other duties in Asia.

All of these presidential aircraft completed their journeys, allowing the historic summit to go ahead. Stock and News has reported that Trump said of the meeting:

“I’m delighted that this trip has also given us the opportunity for this first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the United States, Russia and China….so in that sense, and I think in lots of other ways, we are really making history,”

The chances to see the aging 747-200 Air Force One jets in operation are limited because the planes are approaching 40 years old. The jets have been used by American presidents since the 1990s. They are set to be replaced in 2028 by two 747-8 aircraft, each of which is under 15 years old, following an ongoing conversion program.

It is formally called VC-25B and is expected to cost $5.3 billion. The expense is required to install technology to withstand nuclear electromagnetic pulses, evade surface-to-air missiles, and provide uninterrupted global communications on a civilian aircraft. Air Force One jets feature over 200 miles (321 km) of insulated, military-grade wiring, roughly double what a standard 747 uses.

The unexpected move is raising questions about why the President would make such a decision.

The arrival of the VC-25B will not see the immediate retirement of VC-25A, which is expected to come a year later. In June 2026, White House Communications Director Steven Cheung and Deputy Chief of Staff Dan Scavino posted farewell messages after what was thought to be the final time the president rode on the jets.

There was previously speculation from analysts that the interim 747-8 provided by the Qatari state would not be appropriate for international missions due to its limited modifications and defense systems. It is clear from the plane's use in the China summit that this is not the case.

The 747-200s remain in the fleet in case of mechanical issues, and will serve as Air Force Two until their final retirement in 2029. What will happen to them after is not known, but given their advanced age and the amount of government technology that would need to be removed, they will likely be scrapped or donated to museums.

#6223. Can Rocky Save the World?

Anthony Ippolito (Sylvester Stallone) in I Play Rocky

Sylvester Stallone has been a Hollywood institution for so long — his breakthrough movie Rocky premiered 50 years ago — that his previous underdog status as a struggling actor seems perfectly mythic in the new behind-the-scenes biographical drama I Play Rocky.

The fairy-tale aspect of I Play Rocky comes from its background story. In this, young Stallone (played by Anthony Ippolito) is a virtually homeless outsider, working at a movie theater, who after spending 16 months on writing eight screenplays, joins the creative zeitgeist of 1970s Hollywood, also known as the American Renaissance. It is this personal journey that illuminates the Stallone legend that climaxes with Rocky winning the Academy Award for best picture over such esteemed movies as Taxi Driver, Network, Bound for Glory, and All the President’s Men.

Starting with Stallone practicing elocution (using Walt Whitman’s “I Sing the Body Electric”) to soften his rough New York accent, the film then places him against odds in an era of cultural ferment that included such films as Altman’s The Long Goodbye and Coppola’s The Conversation. (Stallone pays particular attention to the intonation of Coppola’s actors repeating the line “He’d kill us if he found out.”) Screenwriter Peter Gamble doesn’t make that detail ominous but simplifies the life-or-death aspect of Stallone’s career and artistic ambition as part of the wannabe actor’s desperate, working-class consciousness — inspired by viewing the heavyweight championship boxing match between Muhammad Ali and Chuck Wepner. It’s easier to take than the sociological theme in Green Book, the egregious previous film of director Peter Farrelly. I Play Rocky regains the genial humanism of such Farrelly brothers’ movies as Me, Myself and Irene, Stuck on You, and The Ringer, and especially the Farrelly brothers’ script for Outside Providence.

Kiki Seto (Talia Shire) and Anthony Ippolito (Sylvester Stallone) in I Play Rocky

Stallone’s ambition is epitomized by his insistence that the Rocky screenplay he wrote in four days and sold to producers Irwin Winkler and Robert Chartoff can be filmed only starring himself. He demands, “I play Rocky.” That’s not a playground taunt in the milieu of financial bargaining and egotism that’s gleefully depicted by a series of Hollywood types — P. J. Byrne and Toby Kebbell as Winkler and Chartoff, Rob Demery as Joe Frazier, and a standout cameo by Trevor St. John as a self-serious fight coordinator.

In Hollywood’s gladiatorial circus, Stallone’s striving and eventual success become a credible moral victory. He must claim his own identity and career path separately from his worldly father Frank (Matt Dillon gives a moving characterization of a parent’s cynicism, affection, and personal regret). His wife Sasha (AnnaSophie Robb) encourages him: “I’d rather be optimistic and be wrong than pessimistic and be right.” These backstage details (including a hostile producer who dismisses Stallone as “a droopy-eyed hack actor”) make I Play Rocky a credible and appealing saga of Stallone’s indefatigable confidence. The movie rejects the sort of dark, objectionable narcissism that we saw in the Springsteen hagiography Deliver Me from Nowhere.

It is important that the filmmakers accurately measure Rocky’s significance. Farrelly and Gamble mix film history with good sense and humor when portraying wild-eyed director John Avildsen (Jay Duplass) deep in his own world of pragmatic professionalism (“Great art never comes through compromise”). They also capture Stallone’s own, uncanny sense of achieving the proper effect — not so much when Rocky emotes to his manager Mickey as when, in a startling shot, he points to details in a big-screen image of Kirk Douglas in Champion, from 1948.

Putting Rocky in proper perspective is a curatorial feat. It recognizes Stallone’s film as a work of pop lore. Its popularity gave Hollywood the opportunity to ignore scary powerful art like Scorsese’s Taxi Driver in favor of the folk and commercial elements that are easily enjoyed in American culture — although missing from Millennial film culture. Remember: In 1976, Rocky seemed an artificial retread of old boxing films, pilfering the ethnic sentimentality of Marty, On the Waterfront, and Requiem for a Heavyweight as if Muhammad Ali had never happened.

But I Play Rocky works differently. It recalls Stallone’s response to Wepner (“This guy won’t go down!”) to achieve the authentic Millennial pop lore of Better Man, Song Sung Blue, Back 2 America, Power Ballad, and the upcoming Madden. (These restorative myths correct the disappointing Creed sequels that failed to live up to Rocky.) I Play Rocky channels Stallone’s personal perseverance to enlighten our current demoralized sensibilities.

#6222. How The Airbus A321neo, 72% Of The A320neo Family Backlog, Shrinks The Boeing 737 MAX 8 Rivalry To Medium-Demand Routes

Marco Menezes | Shutterstock, Wikimedia Commons, Simple Flying

Brandon's passion for aviation started at a young age. He became involved in the flight simulator and VATSIM communities, which sparked his interest in aviation and eventually led him to earn his private pilot license. Outside of work, he continues to build flight hours, explore new airports, and stay involved in the aviation community.

Airbus’ narrowbody order book now leans heavily on its largest model. At the start of 2026, about 72% of the A320neo family backlog was for the A321neo, and that share has kept climbing. By the end of September, A321neos made up 5,656 of the 7,529 A320neo family aircraft still awaiting delivery, against 1,860 A320neos. That is roughly three of every four aircraft Airbus still owes its customers.

The shift changes what the long-running A320neo versus MAX 8 comparison actually covers. On paper, the MAX 8 offers more maximum seats and slightly more brochure range, while the A320neo offers a wider cabin and a choice of engines. The biggest recent Airbus orders, however, have been for the larger aircraft, and the MAX 10, Boeing’s direct answer to it, has only just been certified. What remains between the A320neo and the MAX 8 is the set of routes where demand does not justify a jet with more than 200 seats.

Order intake explains the backlog. In October alone, Forecast International reported that the A320neo family secured 163 gross orders (comprising 98 A321neos and 65 A320neos). Lessors drove much of that activity, including a firm order for 75 A320neo Family aircraft from Aviation Capital Group (ACG), announced on October 16. However, Airbus and ACG did not disclose the split between A320neo and A321neo aircraft.

Production has followed the same pattern. In full-year 2025, Airbus delivered 793 commercial aircraft, including 607 A320neo-family aircraft, and Air Data News reported that the A321neo accounted for 64% of those handovers. The share has held into 2026. Through October, Airbus had delivered 621 aircraft, and the A321neo alone accounted for 306 deliveries, nearly half of the company’s total for the year. October’s single-aisle handovers were weighted similarly, with 39 aircraft, followed by 15 A320neos.

Engine supply limits how quickly that backlog can come down. Airbus said in February it expects to deliver around 870 commercial aircraft in 2026, as it scaled back its planned production increase for the A320neo family due to shortages of Pratt & Whitney GTF engines. The company now expects A320neo family output to reach 70 to 75 aircraft per month by the end of 2027, stabilizing at 75 thereafter. Former commercial aircraft chief Christian Scherer had said engines arrived “very, very late” throughout 2025, with Airbus expecting the problem to persist into 2026. At that pace, airlines ordering an A321neo today are buying a delivery slot years in the future.

Capacity favors the Boeing, though with a qualifier. Airbus lists the A320neo at 150-180 seats in a typical two-class layout and a maximum of 194, on an overall length of 123 feet, three inches (37.57 meters). Boeing lists the MAX 8 at 162-78 seats in two classes, on a length of 129 feet, eight inches (39.52 meters). The often-quoted 210-seat maximum for the MAX 8 belongs to a sub-variant, which Boeing specifies as the MAX 8-200, with an additional mid-cabin exit. That extra pair of doors raises the evacuation limit enough to allow the denser layout.

Range is close enough that the brochure figures settle little. Airbus says the A320neo flies up to 3,400 nautical miles (6,300 km), while Boeing lists the MAX 8 at 3,500 (6,480) nautical miles. Each manufacturer calculates its maximum under its own assumptions, so the 100-nautical-mile gap tells an airline less about a given route than payload, cabin layout and airport conditions do. The A320neo’s clearer advantage sits inside the aircraft. Airbus lists a maximum cabin width of 12 feet (3.70 meters), and the A320 family’s cross-section has always been wider than the 737’s.

Engines and flight decks separate the two programs more sharply than dimensions do. Airbus offers the A320neo with CFM LEAP-1A or Pratt & Whitney GTF (Geared Turbofan) engines, while every 737 MAX variant uses the LEAP-1B from CFM International. A second engine supplier gives airlines leverage when negotiating an order, although GTF shortages that have slowed Airbus production show the risk of relying on one supplier. In the cockpit, the A320neo uses Airbus’ fly-by-wire controls with sidesticks, and the MAX 8 keeps the conventional control column that 737 pilots have flown for decades.

The A321neo offers more of everything the A320neo does. Airbus lists the aircraft with typical seating of two-class 180-220 seats, with a maximum of 244, and says its Cabin-Flex door configuration increases the jetliner’s maximum certified capacity to 244 seats, while still accommodating Airbus’ modern comfort standard of seats that are at least 18 inches wide. Range extends to 4,000 nautical miles on the standard A321neo, and Airbus says the A321XLR offers up to 4,700 nautical miles.

AEGEAN illustrates how carriers use that flexibility. In March 2025, the Greek airline ordered 8 additional Airbus A321neo aircraft, bringing its A320neo-family commitment to 58. Its earlier A321LR aircraft feature a newly designed passenger cabin, specifically configured for flights to new markets of up to 7.5 hours. In July 2025, AEGEAN added two (2) new Airbus A321XLR (Extra Long Range) aircraft with an even longer range of up to 10.5 hours, with plans for New Delhi service from March and Mumbai from May, taking its order to 60 aircraft.

Lessors have bet heavily on the same aircraft. In July 2025, Avolon placed an order for 90 Airbus aircraft, comprising 15 A330neos and 75 A321neo, bringing Avolon’s total to 79 A330neos and 264 A321neos. Avolon said the aircraft are scheduled to be delivered out to 2033. Leasing companies place aircraft with many airlines over decades, so their orders reflect where they expect demand to settle, and Avolon’s commitment points squarely at the larger model. That pattern explains why the A320neo now makes up a minority of what Airbus still has to build.

Boeing’s direct competitor to the A321neo arrived years late. The FAA certified the MAX 10 on October 20, 2026, clearing the way for deliveries of the largest variant in the 737 MAX family. Boeing described the approval as the final regulatory hurdle in bringing the largest member of the 737 MAX family to operators, following MAX 7 certification in August. Reuters reported that a problem with the anti-ice system on 737 MAX engines that arose in 2023 further delayed certification of the MAX 7 and 10.

On paper, the MAX 10 and A321neo are closer competitors than the A320neo and MAX 8. Boeing lists the MAX 10 at 188–204 seats in two classes, a maximum of 230, and a range of 3,100 (5,740) nautical miles, with a length of 143 feet, 8 inches (43.8 meters). Airbus’ standard A321neo carries up to 244 seats at maximum density and lists 4,000 nautical miles of range, 900 more than the Boeing, before the XLR is counted. Those figures suggest the MAX 10 will compete most directly with the A321neo on high-density domestic and regional routes rather than longer, thinner routes.

Boeing starts with a large order book for the type. It reported 1,555 MAX 10 orders from more than 30 customers at the time of certification, and says the 737-10 represents more than 30 percent of unfilled 737 MAX orders. United holds the largest airline order, with 167 aircraft, according to Cirium data reported by Business Traveller. According to Air Data News, ACG is expected to own the first aircraft delivered, and WestJet is scheduled to operate it. Boeing expects deliveries to begin in the coming months, which makes 2027 the first full year of head-to-head competition between the MAX 10 and the A321neo.

Cost per seat is the metric that reveals all.

The A320neo still sells, even as its share of the backlog shrinks. Airbus’ remaining A320neo backlog stood at 1,860 aircraft at the end of September, and the 65 A320neos ordered in October show that airlines continue to commit to the smaller model. Those aircraft serve markets where a 150- to 180-seat jet fills more reliably than a 200-plus-seat aircraft, including routes that need higher frequency more than additional capacity on each departure.

Boeing’s single-aisle business remains built around the MAX family as a whole. The company says customers have ordered 7,350 737 MAX airplanes to date. Boeing delivered nearly 2,500 as of September. In 2025, Boeing delivered 447 737s, and Air Data News reported that Boeing’s order performance was led overwhelmingly by the 737 MAX, which accounted for 591 gross orders that year, outselling Airbus on net orders.

Read together, the numbers narrow the A320neo versus MAX 8 matchup rather than ending it. Both aircraft still sit at the center of the segment they were designed for, and each manufacturer continues to book orders. The difference is that the higher-capacity market, where Airbus has placed most of its backlog, now has a certified Boeing competitor for the first time. How quickly the MAX 10 can deliver, and how quickly Airbus can clear engine shortages on the A321neo, will shape that segment more than any comparison between the two smaller jets.

Airline baggage fees can vary greatly, and there’s nothing worse than being hit by surprise fees after booking. To add to the challenge, many U.S. airlines raised fees in 2026, with several increases tied to rising fuel costs amid the war in Iran.

At TPG, we try to help readers spend smarter so they can travel better.

This guide summarizes baggage fees by airline, so you know what fees to expect before booking. It also outlines some smart ways to help you avoid them entirely.

Most major U.S. airlines impose several common bag fees, including for checked bags.

As you'll see in the chart below, the fee for your first checked bag typically starts at $45 to $50 each way, but increases quickly as you add a second or third suitcase.

(For flights ticketed on or after Nov. 3, 2026)

This table assumes you’re purchasing a standard domestic economy fare (not basic economy, which costs more on some airlines, such as American) and checking standard luggage that isn’t overweight or oversized. Note that Frontier Airlines considers a bag overweight if it weighs more than 40 pounds, whereas most other carriers set the limit at 50 pounds.

These prices also assume you have no elite status, do not carry a cobranded airline credit card with a checked-bag benefit and are paying for your checked bag at the airport. Fees on some airlines, such as JetBlue, vary by travel date. Bag fees on international flights can differ significantly, especially on long-haul routes.

Note: Some airlines charge less if you pay for your bags online in advance. American and United take $5 off, and JetBlue’s discount can be as much as $15.

Some airlines also charge for carry-on baggage. This is usually limited to low-cost carriers, but you’ll want to check your allowances before your next flight.

Here are the carry-on bag allowances for domestic flights in economy class with most major U.S. airlines:

You’ll notice that most airlines don’t charge a fee for a carry-on bag, but they limit each passenger to one personal item and one carry-on.

A personal item is considered a backpack, laptop bag, camera bag or other small item you can stow underneath the seat in front of you. A carry-on is typically a larger bag or small suitcase that fits in the overhead bin above your seat. Each airline has different dimension limits, so you’ll want to measure your luggage and check your airline’s policy before heading to the airport.

Related: How to tell if your backpack counts as a personal or carry-on item

No major U.S. airline includes a free checked bag with its standard economy fare. (Southwest's higher-priced Choice Extra fare is somewhat of an exception since it allows two free checked bags.) So, regardless of your carrier, expect to pay to check your bag unless you have elite status or the airline's cobranded credit card. Most major airlines charge similar prices — around $45 to $50 for your first checked bag. However, JetBlue now follows a peak and off-peak model, so if you're flying during a peak time, expect to pay more.

Frontier is the least favorable airline when it comes to baggage fees. Not only are its prices the highest, but they also vary by travel dates and purchase time. And while most airlines allow you to check a bag up to 50 pounds, Frontier caps the weight of a standard checked bag at 40 pounds. After that, you’ll pay a pretty penny for overweight bags. Fortunately, the airline offers a baggage calculator to check the cost in advance.

Also note that most airlines charge additional fees for overweight baggage (generally once your bag exceeds 50 pounds). Suitcases over a certain size (often measured in linear inches, length plus width plus height) usually cost extra. Specialty items, like skis or scuba equipment, may also incur additional fees.

Some airlines don't allow you to check luggage with a basic fare, while others offer bundled fares that include checked baggage. Pay close attention to which fare you purchase to minimize luggage fees.

When it comes to basic economy fares, United is the only major U.S. airline (American, Delta and United) that doesn’t include a free carry-on bag on domestic flights. United also charges an additional gate handling fee (on top of the regular baggage fee) if a basic economy passenger brings a full-size bag to the gate that then must be checked.

Paying for your luggage in advance is usually the least expensive option with most airlines. You'll want to pay special attention as some airlines offer a discount during the booking process, while others require you to simply pay for your luggage when checking in for your flight online.

Many U.S. carriers offer a simpler pathway to free checked bags: opening an airline credit card.

Most cobranded cards from U.S. airlines waive the first checked-bag fee on domestic itineraries. In fact, many of these perks extend to companions — up to eight on the same reservation, in some cases. Some cards have annual fees of less than $100.

In other words, you and your entire family could check a bag for free on your next trip simply by holding the right credit card.

For most carriers discussed in this guide, there’s at least one credit card that waives the fee for your first checked bag. Most also extend the favor to additional companions traveling on the same reservation. If you're a frequent flyer with a particular airline, it's worth investigating whether there is a cobranded credit card that suits your needs.

However, perks vary by card and airline; some are more restrictive than others. For example, to get the free first bag with the (see rates and fees), you generally need to buy your ticket using the card.

With others, such as American's Citi cards, you only need to include your loyalty number on the reservation.

The number of permitted companions also varies: The United Explorer Card covers one additional passenger, whereas the allows up to eight traveling companions to check their bags at no additional cost.

Each carrier uses slightly different rules for these policies, but here's a summary of the cards that offer this perk:

Note: You must purchase your flights with the card for bag perks to apply.

Second checked bag free for the cardmember when flying Delta domestically

Note: You must purchase your flights with the card for bag perks to apply.

Note: You must include your Rapid Rewards number when you book for bag perks to apply.

Quest and Club: Two free checked bags on United flights

Note: Must purchase flights with the card for perks to apply.

*The information for the AAdvantage Aviator Red World Elite Mastercard, Frontier Airlines World Mastercard®, JetBlue Plus Card, JetBlue Premier Card and JetBlue Business Card have been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

It's worth pointing out that many of these perks apply automatically based on the loyalty program account associated with the card. However, a few airlines require you to pay for your airfare with the cobranded card to receive the bag fee waiver.

Many travelers aren’t loyal to a given airline, so it may not make sense to hold, say, a United card if you only travel with United once a year. Thankfully, many of the best travel credit cards include credits that can cover checked bag fees when you incur them, and some of them aren’t limited to individual airlines.

Related: The best credit cards with airline fee credits

Additionally, you could consider using a card like the Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card to pay for checked bag fees. The miles you earn on this card can cover travel purchases, and you can use your miles to pay for baggage.

Another option to avoid checked bag fees is to hold elite status with the airline’s frequent flyer program. All airlines mentioned here offer at least one free checked bag to certain elite members.

The vast majority of these tiers — even the lowest ones — allow you to check a bag for free. However, the exact waiver depends on the airline and can vary as you climb the elite status ladder.

For example, all Delta Medallion travelers enjoy at least one free checked bag up to 70 pounds on flights in the U.S. and Canada and 50 pounds on international flights. Within the U.S. and Canada, this jumps to two bags for Gold Medallion members and three for Platinum and Diamond Medallion members.

United also grants Premier travelers a 70-pound weight allowed for checked bags: one bag for Premier Silver, two for Premier Gold, and three for Premier Platinum and Premier 1K.

American follows a similar method for checked bag quantity: one for AAdvantage Gold, two for AAdvantage Platinum and three for AAdvantage Platinum Pro and AAdvantage Executive Platinum. However, unless you're confirmed in business or first class, bags are limited to 50 pounds (except for flights to and from Australia or New Zealand).

Plus, some published policies may offer wiggle room for elite members. For example, elite status holders might be able to get away with a 52-pound bag without tacking on an overweight fee. And, if you have elite status, you may still be able to convince a sympathetic check-in agent to waive the bag fee.

Note that many of these perks extend to partner flights as well. If you hold mid-tier or higher status with an airline in SkyTeam, Star Alliance or Oneworld, you can typically check an extra bag for free on partner airlines.

For more details on the perks of elite status, check out these guides:

When you travel in a premium class of service, you’ll generally enjoy waived checked bag fees — in many cases above and beyond the standard weight allowance as well. These policies typically apply whether you paid cash, points or miles for your ticket, so this can be a great way to use your travel rewards and not have to worry about extra bag fees.

You can check out your operating carrier’s checked baggage page for full details on what’s included for your specific trip.

Here are a few more tricks to avoid checked baggage fees, including overweight or oversize fees.

Most airlines allow you to gate-check carry-on luggage for no additional cost when overhead bin space is tight — and on a fully packed flight, sometimes they'll often require travelers to gate check.

The exceptions are typically low-cost carriers like Frontier, as well as basic economy fares on legacy carriers. Otherwise, most airlines are happy to gate-check just about whatever you’d like — and you may even have luck doing this before boarding starts.

If you gate-check your luggage, ensure the airline checks it through to baggage claim. However, you must claim some items — such as strollers, wheelchairs and even rolling carry-ons on regional planes — at the gate upon arrival.

As punitive as airline baggage policies can be, some helpful exceptions exist. For example, most U.S. carriers let you check skis, snowboards and boots as a single checked bag — even if your skis are in a different bag from your boots. The same often holds for hockey equipment, which typically doesn’t require an additional fee as long as it’s within the standard weight allotment.

Before you go to the airport, take a screenshot of the rules in case you encounter an agent who is unfamiliar with uncommon checked items.

Check-in agents at the curb are often contractors, not airline employees. So, they may have less incentive to strictly enforce the airline’s baggage rules. Additionally, some locations may not have scales to weigh the bags.

In the U.S., carry-on weight restrictions are rarely enforced. So, when packing for your next vacation, put heavy items in your carry-on bag rather than risk paying for overweight checked bags.

For less than $10, you can find a small, lightweight scale to weigh your luggage. These scales are typically quite accurate and will help you stay under your desired weight. You’ll also avoid being that person repacking their bags at the airport and holding up the line.

Beyond the above strategies, many airlines waive checked bag fees for all customers when traveling to specific areas. For example, American Airlines offers free checked baggage on flights to select destinations including Argentina, Brazil, China, India and Japan. This also extends to all transatlantic travels. And, if you’re flying American to either Australia or New Zealand, your free bag can weigh up to 70 pounds.

Basic economy passengers may still pay on some routes, such as transatlantic flights, and there may be seasonal restrictions for certain locales.

Regardless of the airline you’re flying, be sure to research your baggage allowance ahead of time so you know what to expect — and so you don’t encounter an expensive surprise at the airport.

Bag fees are an unfortunate reality of air travel in 2026. In certain situations, your bags could wind up costing hundreds of dollars beyond the original price of the ticket. So, carefully consider baggage policies before jumping on that “great deal.”

If there’s a cobranded credit card or an easy way to earn elite status (one that offers waived baggage fees) for the particular airline you’re flying, it might be worth looking into those options. You might find that the annual fee on your credit card is far less than the checked-bag fees for your family over the course of the year.

#6218. Britt bill would launch national office to combat financial fraud

Britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

A bill introduced by Sen. Katie Britt on Wednesday aims to combat a rising diversity of financial fraud by unifying the U.S. effort to fight it.

The draft bill would establish a National Office for Scam and Fraud Prevention in the White House that would coordinate federal, state and private sector efforts. It is aimed at ensuring that federal agencies, law enforcement, financial institutions, telecommunications and technology companies and other groups work together, according to an overview from Britt.

The new office would promote intelligence sharing across the public and private sectors, coordinate consumer education efforts and improve assistance for victims.

Britt, R-Ala., said the effort is needed because fraudsters operate nimbly utilizing social media while taking advantage of fragmented or disorganized responses from individual companies and government agencies.

“This effort is about bringing everyone to the table and making sure our response keeps pace with the criminals who are exploiting new technologies and gaps between sectors,” she said in a statement. “When we work together to identify threats earlier and share information more effectively, we can better protect American families and businesses.”

The office would develop a “lexicon of fraud” so that terms for different kinds of scams are standardized between various federal law enforcement agencies to promote a “whole-of-government response,” a Britt aide said.

The office also would work to broaden the approach to combating fraud beyond just having financial institutions reimburse victims. It would tap telecommunications and technology companies to address fraud at its source, such as rip-offs that start as text messages, social media posts or online advertisements.

Britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. She is the sponsor of a bill that would allow state, local and tribal law enforcement agencies to use federal grant funding to investigate financial fraud, particularly scams targeted at the elderly.

The measure highlights the prevalence of "pig butchering," a common technique where a predator cultivates a personal relationship with a victim over many months to extract the most cash.

The House passed its version of the bill in September with overwhelming bipartisan support. The House sponsor is Rep. Zach Nunn, R-Iowa.

Senior financial abuse also was the focus of a bill the House passed in an overwhelming 414-2 vote in June. The legislation, sponsored by Rep. Ann Wagner, R-Mo., would codify Securities and Exchange Commission guidance that permits mutual funds and their agents to postpone the sale of securities if there is a reasonable belief that financial exploitation of someone who is elderly or disabled is occurring

It's not clear whether the Senate will take action on these bills or Britt's by the end of the year.

“If it doesn’t get through in the lame duck, it will continue to be a priority in the 120th [Congress],” the Britt aide said.

#6215. UBI Breeds Dependence and Restricts Opportunity

The new Democratic Congress should walk away from the destructive path of this policy.

Democrats seized control of Congress, in part by focusing on affordability and the economy. An AP-NORC survey conducted just before the election found that both were ranked top issues for registered voters, outpacing the next most important issue, health care, by about 15 percentage points.

The new Democratic Congress will presumably pursue policies that are advertised as ways to reduce the cost of living. One idea they should reject is universal basic income (UBI). Leftists have long pushed for UBI, and the idea is gaining stream among tech leaders. It’s a policy that would backfire by reigniting inflation and ultimately harming those it attempts to help.

Joshua Bandoch is a research fellow with the Competitive Enterprise Institute, a free-market public-policy organization based in Washington, D.C.

Kevin Corinth is the Daniel C. Searle Chair and a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute.

#6214. Surprise: Aer Lingus Unveils First-Ever Premium Economy, Coming To 10 A330s

Aer Lingus is getting on the premium economy hype. The Irish flag carrier has today announced it will introduce the cabin for the first time on 10 of its Airbus A330s, which will also feature new business and economy cabins (the product won’t be coming to the Airbus A321LR/XLR fleet).

This is quite a big change, and one that should give it a leg up in the highly competitive trans-Atlantic market.

The cabin will feature just four rows with 28 seats in a 2-3-2 configuration. That’s about average when compared to other premium economy cabins. The narrow fuselage of the A330 means there’s only room for three seats in the middle section, rather than the four many other airlines offer.

As for the soft product, Aer Lingus promises three-course dining, drinks throughout the flight, a pillow and blanket, an amenity kit, and noise-reducing (not noise-canceling) headphones.

I actually really like the design and color scheme. It’s modern, looks elegant and premium, and most importantly of all for the airline of the Emerald Isle, the colors are quintessentially Irish.

Aer Lingus says premium economy fares will start from 700 Euros one-way, putting a return trip at around 1,400 Euros. That works out to around $1,534, and a few hundred dollars cheaper than United’s nonstop fares from Newark (EWR) to Dublin (DUB).

We’ll have to wait until October 1 next year to try Aer Lingus’ new premium economy out for ourselves. The airline hasn’t yet announced which routes will get the product first, but we should find out in the coming months.

The good news is, they’ll operate on many of the airline’s 18 nonstop routes from Dublin to the United States.

As a small, almost boutique-style airline with just 63 aircraft, Aer Lingus must remain competitive, especially in the saturated transatlantic market in which it predominantly operates. The addition of premium economy bridges the large gap between economy and business, and should open the airline up to a potential new customer base who’ve never flown it before.

I’ll be attending an event in Dublin tonight, so I should be back with more images and extra info soon!

What do you make of Aer Lingus’ new premium economy?

#6213. Aer Lingus Retrofitting A330s With New Business, Premium Economy, Economy Cabins

It’s not just Aer Lingus’ premium economy stealing the headlines in Ireland today. Expected to fly passengers for the first time on October 1, 2027, the new cabins are part of a comprehensive Airbus A330 tip-to-tail retrofit that will include new business and economy cabins. We covered the premium economy cabin in a separate article story.

The same 10 Airbus A330s that will get the airline’s new premium economy will also get a swanky new business class. The airline’s Airbus A321XLRs aren’t included in this cabin update.

Aer Lingus opted for its take on the ever-popular Collins Elevation suite. There’ll be 28 seats in a 1-2-1 configuration that stretch out to 78 inches long when in lie-flat mode.

The color palette of Irish greens, whites, and light wood gives the seat an elegant yet distinctly non-corporate feel. It’s a thumbs-up from me.

In terms of updated tech, each seat has 4K HD screens (in all cabins) as well as wireless and USB-C charging. While nothing revolutionary, these touches will significantly modernize Aer Lingus A330 cabins.

Aer Lingus is also introducing a self-service bar stocked with snacks and drinks. I wonder if this will include Champagne…

The airline will also serve up a whole new in-flight dining experience featuring dishes inspired by both Irish ingredients and its transatlantic destinations.

It wouldn’t be a full retrofit without sprucing up economy.

Per the renderings, Aer Lingus has done a great job again with the cabin’s look and feel. The emerald green Shamrocks are a lovely touch.

Seats are configured in the A330’s classic 2-4-2 configuration — a favorite for those traveling in pairs.

While the recline looks a bit modest here, the seat’s thickness looks like it’ll provide more support than some of those ultra-thin, rigid seats airlines are sneaking in these days.

The six-way adjustable headrests should also mean less head-wobbling when catching some shut-eye.

The curved design of the seat backs should hopefully mean noticeably more knee space.

Aer Lingus is also upping its food and beverage ante for economy passengers. In addition to a snack bar, a new mid-flight snack will be offered.

A retrofit program like this was essential for Aer Lingus to remain competitive in the transatlantic market. The introduction of premium economy was a great move, especially since the cabin is known to be highly profitable.

Aer Lingus has also done a great job of matching the Irish color scheme and sleek design across all cabins, which is more than can be said for some airlines these days. 😉

What do you make of Aer Lingus’ new A330 cabins?

#6212. Democrats nominate Jeffries to be House speaker, a historic first

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., flanked by House Minority Whip Katherine M. Clark, D-Mass., and House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., hold a press conference in the Capitol after the House Democratic leadership elections on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries won a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday setting him up to be the nation’s first Black speaker of the House, a historic step that follows Democrats’ staggering election wins earlier this month.

Jeffries, who had called for a recorded vote of the more than 250-member caucus that will serve in the next Congress despite facing no announced opponent, won decisively, 251-11. The margin suggests Jeffries will easily surpass the necessary 218 votes he will need on the House floor when the full chamber votes in January.

“It's a high honor and a distinct privilege to stand before the American people today as a Democratic nominee to be the next Speaker of the United States House of Representatives,” Jeffries said at a press conference following the election.

While Jeffries celebrates his win, he has continued to put an emphasis on unity before he faces what has been deemed the toughest job in Washington. Democrats’ massive majority will give him some margin for maneuvering as he balances the priorities of a complex caucus ranging from moderates to progressives.

“Our job is to fight MAGA extremism, not each other,” Jeffries responded when asked about the 11 defections and what they mean for the next Congress. “Fight MAGA extremism, and to get big things done for the American people, and that is what we are going to accomplish together, beginning on January 3rd.”

Seven of the 11 members who intended to vote against Jeffries released a statement saying that conversations with leadership are still “ongoing” and that there is “work to be done,” but noting there has been “meaningful progress.” The seven included Reps.- elect Darializa Avilia Chavelier, D-N.Y., Adam Hamawy, D-N.J., Frederick Haynes, D-Texas, Melat Kiros, D-Colo., Donovan McKinney, D-Mich., Chris Rabb, D-Pa., and Claire Valdez, D-N.Y.

“Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these issues,” they wrote. “We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations.”

Newly elected House Democrats will meet with former President Barack Obama Wednesday night, where party unity will also be a likely topic.

“This is the beginning of a new bargain, a new politics where hard work is honored and where people's voice is paramount, and where we have more confidence in the future than nostalgia for the past,” House Minority Whip Katherine M. Clark, D-Mass., said at the press conference.

Rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., who made history two decades ago as the nation’s first female speaker, arrived for the vote chanting “Hakeem Jeffries!”, reflecting party leaders’ desire to start the long morning of balloting on a positive note.

Jeffries' nomination followed the election of current Democratic Caucus Vice Chairman Ted Lieu, D-Calif., to serve as the caucus chair in the next Congress. Separate votes followed Wednesday morning, keeping Jeffries' leadership team intact: Clark, as the new majority leader and Democratic Caucus Chairman Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., as majority whip.

At his news conference, Jeffries noted that Clark was also making history as the first woman ever to serve in the position. Aguilar will also be the first Latino to serve as majority whip.

“We've been looking at people's talents, not a particular gender or race, and I think that's a good thing,” outgoing Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, D-Md., a former majority leader, told reporters ahead of the election.

“I think Hakeem Jeffries is going to be a good speaker,” Hoyer continued. “He has the confidence of the caucus, and he has a good leadership team that is close knit and very organized.”

Jeffries expressed confidence in the weeks leading up to his securing the top Democratic spot in the House, brushing aside questions about incoming members who had said they remained “undecided” ahead of the election.

Pelosi was nominated for speaker by acclamation ahead of her first election to the position in 2007. But Jeffries’ allies portrayed his decision to move forward with a recorded vote as a show of strength after a group of incoming progressives had floated forcing a recorded vote in the internal leadership race.

The entire leadership team will be tested despite their numerical advantage over Republicans by the same internal tensions facing Senate Democrats, where current Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., is being challenged for leadership of the majority by Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md.

Jeffries said Tuesday that the approach to the caucus vote mirrored the caucus’ 2018 transition from minority to majority, giving members an opportunity to weigh in on who was best positioned to lead based on their “track record, experience and vision.”

Jeffries has already outlined some of his top priorities of his speakership such as a hefty healthcare agenda, immigration legislation, and a multitude of investigations into the Trump administration.

He also signaled Wednesday another area where his party’s restive base is likely to close ranks: oversight.

“House Democrats will hold the crooks accountable, not for partisan reasons, but for patriotic ones,” he said at his news conference.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Chase Ultimate Rewards points to be worth 1.7 cents each, meaning the 100,000 points are worth $1,700 to me, which is among the best bonuses out there. There are lots of great uses of Chase points, as they can be transferred to all kinds of useful airline and hotel partners.

Chase Ultimate Rewards partners with programs like Air Canada Aeroplan, Air France-KLM Flying Blue, British Airways Club, United MileagePlus, Virgin Atlantic Flying Club, World of Hyatt, and more. If you want to cash out Chase points (which I wouldn’t recommend), you can get one cent of value per point, meaning the 100,000 points would be worth $1,000.

Just to give some examples of possible uses of the points, you could transfer 34,000 points to Iberia Club for a one-way Iberia business class ticket from Boston to Madrid, or 60,000 points to Flying Blue for a one-way Air France or KLM business class ticket from Miami to Paris. You can stretch your points even further by taking advantage of transfer bonuses.

Let me emphasize that the Chase Ink Preferred 100K bonus is the best publicly available sign-up bonus that’s currently available on the card, and it has been the standard offer since November 2025. How do the previous Chase Ink Preferred offers compare, though?

As you can see, the Ink Business Preferred sign-up bonus on the card has varied from 80,000 points to 120,000 points, and the current bonus of 100,000 points is 10,000 points better than the previous offer, which was for up to 90,000 points.

Everyone has to decide for themselves if it’s worth waiting for the possibility of another welcome bonus of over 100,000 points. Personally I probably wouldn’t wait, since we have no reason to believe such an offer is returning soon. Furthermore, with the card’s useful points categories for spending, there’s potentially quite an opportunity cost to waiting. But still, if you’re in no rush, it could be worth waiting.

When it comes to getting approved for the Chase Ink Preferred Card and earning the welcome bonus, what rules should you be aware of? Well, there are the card specific policies, and then also the more generic Chase policies. When you pull up the application, you’ll see the following terms:

The new cardmember bonus may not be available to you if you have ever had this card. We may also consider factors pertinent to your business in determining your bonus eligibility.

As you can see, officially the welcome bonus may not be available to you if you currently have this card, or if you’ve had it in the past. However, eligibility for the card (including the bonus) is unrelated to whether you have any other Chase business card.

In other words, you’re eligible for this card, including the bonus, if you have other cards from Chase, including cards in the business lineup. Speaking of which, those cards have some amazing bonuses as well, which are worth considering:

Beyond that, there are some general Chase rules to be aware of:

While Chase business cards can be tough to get approved for, they offer such fantastic bonuses and perks, so it’s worth the effort, in my opinion. Furthermore, it’s nice how the eligibility requirements aren’t too strict in terms of qualifying for the bonus.

The Chase Ink Preferred Card has a $95 annual fee (with no cost for additional employee cards), and offers all kinds of amazing perks that make it worth holding onto. Among other things, here’s what makes the card so valuable:

Let me acknowledge that the Ink Preferred isn’t right for everyone. As I see it, the Ink Preferred is all about the rewards structure and the strong purchase and travel protection, while also having a reasonable cost. If you’re looking for airport lounge access or a card with all kinds of premium perks and credits, then consider the Sapphire Reserve Business, which many people will find to be worthwhile for the Chase Sapphire Lounge access, Priority Pass membership, travel credits, and more.

The Chase Ink Preferred Card is one of the best business cards out there, and if you’re eligible for the card, there’s lots of merit to applying.

Not only does the card have a big bonus, but it’s worth holding onto for the great rewards structure, excellent protection benefits, and the ability to maximize other cards in the Chase ecosystem. With the changes we’ve seen to other Chase cards in recent times, this card is arguably even more compelling than in the past.

Do you have the Chase Ink Preferred Card, and if so, what has your experience been?

Aer Lingus announced a major overhaul of its Airbus A330 fleet, modernizing the interior of the aging jets with a complete nose-to-tail retrofit.

The Irish flag carrier will install its first-ever Premium Economy cabin, along with all-new lie-flat business class suites and updated economy seats. The airline said it will also continue to offer free Starlink Wi-Fi on the refurbished planes.

The retrofit will come to 10 of the airline's A330 jets, Aer Lingus said in an announcement. The airline has a total of 10 A330-300 jets in service, along with two long-range A330-200s, according to Planespotters.net. It was not immediately clear what would happen to the two A330s that are not included in the retrofit.

Review: Flying Aer Lingus business class across the Atlantic in its current A330 configuration

Aer Lingus described the project as one of its "most significant investments in the onboard customer experience in more than a decade."

"Our ambition here is simple," Aer Lingus CEO Lynn Embleton said in a statement. "We want to give our customers greater choice, comfort and connectivity, while creating an experience that feels unmistakably Aer Lingus."

The retrofitted jets will fly transatlantic routes to North America, the airline said, starting on Oct. 1 with flights EI104 and EI105 between Dublin Airport (DUB) and New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK).

Let's take a closer look at the retrofit.

Premium economy cabins have become much more widespread among airlines over the past decade, with carriers capitalizing on customers who are willing to pay a premium for more comfort, but are still price-sensitive and won't pay for business class.

Aer Lingus is late to the trend, but clearly ready to commit. The airline will install four rows of premium economy seats in a 2-3-2 configuration for a total of 28 seats.

Premium economy will also have its own cabin service, with a three-course meal and drinks throughout the flight, along with amenity kits, bedding, and "noise-reducing" headphones to use during the flight.

The new cabin will be priced squarely in between coach and business class, with fares starting at €700 each way, or about $768.

The business-class cabin will see a major upgrade, bringing a fresh new product to replace one that has become dated.

The cabin will feature 28 business-class suites across seven rows in a 1-2-1 layout, giving every passenger direct aisle access. That's two fewer seats than on the current A330-300, but a big improvement since alternating rows in the existing cabin are configured in a sort of 1-2-2 layout.

Aer Lingus says that it also plans to revamp its onboard dining experience to showcase "seasonal Irish ingredients and contemporary culinary influences," although the airline did not share specifics. There will also be a self-service bar with drinks and snacks in the cabin.

The economy cabin will also see new seats with a handful of features aimed at keeping passengers comfortable on long flights, including a six-way adjustable leather headrest.

Every economy seat in the 2-4-2 cabin will have a 4K seat-back screen with Bluetooth connectivity for headphones, plus USB-C charging. A new in-flight snack station will have bites available after the main meal service.

The design of economy and the entire plane is recognizably Aer Lingus, with a palette heavy on greens and whites with customized mood lighting to accent the on-board experience.

Aer Lingus has offered a pleasant business-class product with stellar on-board service and decent availability, but there's no denying that its "hard product" has fallen behind the times. The new refresh will bring the airline up to snuff with competitors, and should elevate the overall product to match the service provided by the excellent cabin crew.

The new premium economy cabin, meanwhile, offers travelers a new way to fly to Ireland and beyond with more space for a more comfortable journey, while helping Aer Lingus capture an increasingly important passenger segment.

Overall, we're excited to see the new Aer Lingus hit the skies next fall!

#6209. World Of Hyatt 2027 Updates: Milestone Rewards From 10 Nights, New Rewards, And More

World of Hyatt members can expect more flexibility and choice from January 1, 2027. Highlights of the update include earning Milestone Rewards sooner, a bunch of new Milestone Rewards, and more flexibility when redeeming rewards and paying for stays. There’s actually no huge catch, and the changes I learned about last night on an intimate call with the Hyatt team are genuinely member-focused.

The update follows the new Hyatt-Delta relationship, which also launched this week.

Starting January 1, 2027, World of Hyatt members will start enjoying Milestone Rewards after 10 nights stayed or 20,000 base points. That’s great news for relatively infrequent Hyatt guests (like myself), who will no longer have to stay 20 nights or earn 35,000 base points to earn their first Milestone Reward.

At 10 nights or 20,000 base points, members will be able to choose from:

Milestone Rewards will be unlocked at every ten nights, up to 150 nights.

Not only is it about to become quicker to earn Milestone Rewards, but there’ll also be new awards to choose from each level. Here are a few examples of the 20+ new rewards:

The downside of free parking becoming a Milestone Reward means that World of Hyatt members who earn Globalist from 2027 onwards will no longer enjoy it as a permanent status perk on award stays. This will be a notable downgrade to Globalists who value their parking perk.

Hyatt has published a handy new infographic with all the details.

There are also two more important Milestone Reward changes to note, both of which aren’t such positive news:

For the first time, World of Hyatt members will be able to stack multiple awards on a single stay. For example, you can use a Suite Upgrade Voucher, a Guest of Honor Award, and claim free parking, all on the same stay.

All awards will also expire after 365 of being issued. That’s great for awards that used to only last 180 days.

I think this could be my favorite update. Hyatt is enhancing its Pay My Way option to allow guests to choose how to pay for each night of a stay. As someone who struggles to rack up Hyatt points (Hyatt isn’t a transfer partner of any cards in the U.K.), this should certainly streamline booking stays for me.

The booking page will display each award applied to each individual night and provide guests with a drop-down menu to select how they’d like to pay for each night.

At a time when we’re plagued with loyalty program devaluations, these changes coming to World of Hyatt appear to be a genuinely positive slew of updates. Even when you consider some of the less favorable updates, like Globalists losing free parking and some award expiration dates being limited to 365 days, the changes will be positive overall for the vast majority of World of Hyatt members.

What do you make of these World of Hyatt changes?

There are some definite positives to the news but also several losses (free parking, expiration date of SUA and GOH awards being much more limited, no more automatic My Hyatt Concierge) which make the changes more of a mixed bag and not exactly "no huge catch" and "genuinely member-focused." (again, ick on that last statement).
