#6196. Buy Avianca Lifemiles With 145% Bonus (1.35 Cents Each): Worth It?

The avianca lifemiles program is currently offering a limited time 145% bonus on purchased miles. With this, lifemiles members can purchase miles for as little as 1.35 cents each. Is this a good deal?

I find lifemiles to be one of the more useful frequent flyer programs for redeeming miles, thanks to the ability to redeem for long haul premium cabin Star Alliance awards. However, let me emphasize that the program doesn’t always have access to the same award space as other Star Alliance programs, so you’ll want to do your own research, based on the travel you’re trying to plan.

I’d only consider buying miles with a very specific use in mind. For what it’s worth, I don’t get any sort of kickback if you buy miles — I just want to make OMAAT readers aware of the deals that are available.

Link: Buy avianca lifemiles with this promotion with a 145% bonus

Between November 18 and November 21, 2026, the avianca lifemiles program is offering a bonus on purchased miles. While different members may be targeted for different offers, the standard offer that I see across accounts is for a bonus of up to 145%, structured as follows:

You’ll of course want to check your account to see what offer you’re targeted for, as it could be different. It’s common for lifemiles to promote one amount, and then actually offer a bigger bonus. Note that nowadays lifemiles promotions are generally targeted, so different members may see different offers, and on top of that, some members may not see any offers at all.

Ordinarily you can buy avianca lifemiles for 3.3 cents each, before any discounts or bonuses. That means that if you purchased 200,000 lifemiles (pre-bonus) with a 145% bonus (assuming you’re eligible for that), you’d receive a total of 490,000 lifemiles for $6,600, which is a cost of 1.35 cents per mile. That’s inclusive of all taxes and fees.

If you wanted to buy as few miles as possible at the possible price, you’d want to buy exactly 51,000 miles at a cost of $1,683, and that would get you 122,500 lifemiles.

Unfortunately this isn’t quite the best promotion we’ve seen from the program, as we’ve seen bigger percentage bonuses in the past. However, it’s anyone’s guess when we see a bigger offer again.

The lifemiles program lets members purchase up to 500,000 miles per account per calendar year, before factoring in any bonuses. However, the limit per transaction is 200,000 miles, so if you really wanted to max out the number of miles you can buy, you’d need to make multiple transactions.

When members purchase lifemiles, they typically post nearly instantly. However, in rare cases it can take up to 72 hours for them to post. Mileage purchases are non-refundable, so once you make the purchase, it’s final.

When the lifemiles program does offer a promotion on purchased miles, it’s typically in the range of 120-130%. So this is within that range. Personally I’d buy points based on when you’re ready to redeem them, rather than the exact cost. After all, the cost to buy points with a 120% bonus vs. 125% bonus vs. 130% bonus doesn’t differ that much.

Below is a chart with some of the recent promotions we saw from the program, before this one.

Mileage purchases are processed directly by avianca lifemiles, which means the purchase of miles does qualify as airfare spending. Therefore you’ll want to consider using one of the below cards for your purchase, since you’d earn bonus points for airfare purchases.

For context, avianca is in the Star Alliance, which means you can redeem lifemiles on all Star Alliance airlines without any fuel surcharges. Really this is the core value proposition of buying lifemiles, since this is a great way to book Star Alliance premium cabin seats at a huge discount. Check out my guide on how to redeem lifemiles for ideas on how to redeem these miles.

With a specific use in mind, this lifemiles promotion can be a great value, whether you’re looking at traveling in first class on All Nippon Airways, or are looking at traveling in business class on a countless number of airlines.

Everyone has to crunch the numbers for themselves and decide whether this makes sense or not.

Let me again emphasize that in some cases, lifemiles doesn’t have access to the same award availability as Star Alliance partners, for better or worse. Sometimes lifemiles doesn’t have access to partner awards that other programs do have access to, and other times the inverse is true.

That’s why I always recommend doing some “dummy” award searches before buying miles, so you can get a sense of how award availability lines up with your needs. Keep in mind that you can get even more value from the program with a lifemiles+ subscription, and lifemiles’ credit cards offer a discount on that.

Everyone will value mileage currencies differently. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider avianca lifemiles to be worth 1.3 cents each. That’s based on the redemption values on Star Alliance partners, as there’s tons of value to be had. I tend to value miles very conservatively, so if you’re maximizing miles you should be able to get way more value than that.

Miles with the lifemiles program don’t expire as long as you accrue some miles at least once every 12 months. Any mileage earning activity, including buying miles, will extend the expiration of your miles. However, redeeming miles as such doesn’t extend the expiration of your miles.

If you’re looking to earn lifemiles, the good news is that there are lots of options beyond outright buying them. Specifically, avianca lifemiles is partners with several bank currencies, including Amex Membership Rewards, Bilt Rewards, Capital One, and Citi ThankYou, so there are lots of ways to pick up these miles.

For purchases through November 21, 2026, the avianca lifemiles program is offering a promotion on purchased miles. Different members may be eligible for different offers, though it appears that the standard offer is for up to a 145% bonus, which is an opportunity to acquire miles for 1.35 cents each. This has the potential to represent a solid value, though I’d only recommend buying miles with a specific, short term use in mind.

#6195. Buy JetBlue TrueBlue Points With 125% Bonus (1.43 Cents Each): Worth It?

JetBlue is currently offering a limited time 125% bonus on purchased points. With this, TrueBlue members can purchase points for as little as 1.43 cents each. Is this a good deal?

Let’s take a look at the details — so that I don’t bury the lede, let me say that I’d only recommend taking advantage of this JetBlue buy points offer with a specific use in mind, and primarily if you intend to redeem on partner airlines.

Link: Buy JetBlue TrueBlue points with this promotion with a 125% bonus

Between 12AM ET on November 18 and 11:59PM ET on December 31, 2026, JetBlue TrueBlue is offering a bonus on purchased points, which is close to being in line with the best offers from the program.

JetBlue TrueBlue is offering up to a 125% bonus on purchasing points. The offer is structured as follows, with three tiers of bonuses:

Let me emphasize that this appears to be the standard offer, though sometimes different members are targeted for different offers. You’ll want to log into your TrueBlue account to see what you’re eligible for.

JetBlue ordinarily allows TrueBlue members to purchase up to 200,000 points per calendar year. However, during this promotion, that cap has been increased to 300,000 points.

JetBlue ordinarily charges 3.0 cents per purchased point, before the 7.5% federal excise tax. After factoring in the federal excise tax, the standard cost is 3.225 cents per purchased point.

With this JetBlue points sale, you’d pay the following amounts per purchased point, factoring in the bonus:

If you wanted to purchase the fewest possible points at the best possible price, you’d want to purchase a total of 45,000 points (20,000 points plus 25,000 bonus points) at a cost of $645, which gets you the cost of 1.43 cents per point, including all taxes.

Meanwhile if you wanted to purchase the most possible points, you’d want to purchase a total of 675,000 points (300,000 points plus 375,000 bonus points) at a cost of $9,675, which gets you the same cost per point.

Officially, JetBlue states that it can take up to 72 hours for purchased points to post. However, in practice (based on my test experience of buying points), they’ll typically post almost instantly. There’s no guarantee of that, though.

Note that the purchase of JetBlue points is non-refundable, so only make a purchase if you have a specific use in mind. Furthermore, the purchase of JetBlue points doesn’t count toward Mosaic elite status, in case that’s a consideration.

When JetBlue does offer a promotion on purchased points, it’s typically in the range of 120-130%. So this is within that range. Personally I’d buy points based on when you’re ready to redeem them, rather than the exact cost. After all, the cost to buy points with a 120% bonus vs. 125% bonus vs. 130% bonus doesn’t differ that much.

Below is a chart with some of the recent promotions we saw from the program, before this one.

JetBlue TrueBlue points purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as an airfare purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. That means if you use a JetBlue credit card to pay for your purchase, it wouldn’t code as a JetBlue purchase.

Therefore I’d recommend using a card on which you’re trying to reach a minimum spending requirement, or otherwise, a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending. See my guide to the best credit cards for buying points.

JetBlue TrueBlue has become more interesting on the redemption front in recent years, and there are definitely some ways to get outsized value. For that matter, in some cases people may find value in topping off their points balance, in order to have enough points for a redemption.

Let’s look at the opportunities to redeem TrueBlue points, first for travel on JetBlue, and then for travel on partner airlines. For what it’s worth, based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider TrueBlue points to be worth 1.3 cents each.

When it comes to redeeming on JetBlue, TrueBlue is a revenue based frequent flyer program. That means the cost of an award redemption is correlated to how much a ticket would cost in cash, though it’s not always a consistent cent per point value.

In my experience, you’ll typically get around 1.3-1.5 cents per TrueBlue point toward the cost of a ticket on JetBlue in economy.

Just as an example, take a JetBlue flight from Boston to Fort Lauderdale, which costs $334 if paying cash. If redeeming TrueBlue points, you’d pay 22,500 points plus $5.60 in taxes & fees, meaning you’re getting around 1.46 cents of value per point.

As another example, take a JetBlue flight from Boston to San Francisco, which has both economy and Mint business class. If paying cash, you’d pay $198 or $676. If redeeming points, you’d pay 14,200 points or 47,300 points, plus $5.60 in taxes & fees, meaning you’re getting around 1.35-1.42 cents of value per point.

As you can see, these are situations where you probably shouldn’t buy TrueBlue points. For example, there’s no reason to acquire 14,200 points for 1.43 cents each, for a total cost of $203 (plus the $5.60 in taxes & fees), when you could instead just outright buy the ticket for $198.

One thing to keep in mind is that if you have JetBlue’s most premium card, you can get a 15% award rebate, so maybe there is a little upside there.

JetBlue TrueBlue has gotten better about adding redemptions on partner airlines in recent times, including on Qatar Airways, Condor, and United Airlines. We’re also now seeing redemptions added on China Airlines. There’s definitely some value to be had here.

For example, you could redeem just 47,400 points for Condor business class one-way from Frankfurt to Toronto. That’s an amazing opportunity to buy points and immediately get outsized value.

As another example, you could redeem 29,600 points for Qatar Airways business class one-way from Munich to Doha. Given the points acquisition costs we’re talking about, that’s an amazing value.

One caveat I’d just like to add is that partner award availability can be really tough to come by, so only buy points if you have an understanding of what that availability is like.

As I see it, the decision of whether to buy points from a particular loyalty program comes down both to how valuable that currency is, and it also comes down to how many ways there are to acquire the currency. So that’s why it’s worth mentioning that JetBlue TrueBlue points are really easy to acquire.

At this point, JetBlue partners with virtually all transferable points currencies, so you can earn TrueBlue points through Amex Membership Rewards, Bilt Rewards, Capital One Rewards, Chase Ultimate Rewards, Citi ThankYou, Wells Fargo, etc. Bilt, Chase, Citi, and Wells Fargo, have 1:1 transfer ratios, while Amex has a 5:4 ratio, and Capital One has a 5:3 ratio.

Another option is to apply for JetBlue’s co-branded credit cards, which often have large welcome bonuses. Those points of course won’t post anywhere close to instantly, but it’s a good strategy for building up your TrueBlue points balance over time.

So there’s no shortage of opportunities to earn TrueBlue points — it’s just a function of whether you’d rather part with cash or a points currency.

Through December 31, 2026, JetBlue is selling TrueBlue points with up to a 125% bonus, an opportunity to buy points for as little as 1.43 cents each. I’d only buy JetBlue points with a specific use in mind. There’s value to be had in some situations, such as if you have a particular Qatar Airways or Condor award you want to book, and there’s availability.

Anyone plan on buying JetBlue TrueBlue points with a bonus?

#6194. FCC pick advanced by Senate Commerce after Democratic boycott

Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, talks with reporters after the Senate luncheons in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

The fight over partisan balance on the Federal Communications Commission snarled a Senate markup Wednesday morning as Republicans advanced a controversial nomination despite a Democratic boycott in an attempt to deny a quorum.

Republicans on the Commerce Committee voted unanimously to advance the nomination of Danielle Thumann Severs, a senior counsel to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, to be a member of the commission, alongside several transportation and communications bills.

The fate of the nominations and bills could ultimately be decided via a challenge on the Senate floor, according to a Democratic committee staffer, speaking on condition of anonymity.

In a statement Wednesday morning, committee Democrats, led by ranking member  Maria Cantwell of Washington, said they objected to Thumann Severs’ nomination without a Democratic “pair” nomination and referenced a letter they sent to Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, on Monday requesting the nomination be removed from the agenda.

“Commissioner Anna Gomez could be re-nominated with all swiftness, as we have called for numerous times,” the group wrote. “This is not a problem we created, but a problem that the White House can solve.”

Thumann Severs, if confirmed, would give the FCC three Republican members and one Democrat, Gomez. The three Republicans could then constitute a quorum on the commission, allowing President Donald Trump to potentially fire Gomez. The commission generally has five members, three of the president’s party and two in the minority.

Cruz said at the markup that there is nothing in the law that requires moving nominees in pairs, and that committee Republicans would continue their work on what he called a nomination that followed a “typical process.”

“Democrats will control the Senate, unfortunately, in January,” Cruz said. “But today is November 18th. The American people elected each of us to fulfill our duties, including advice and consent, for our full terms.”

Related: Threats to broadcasters hang over FCC nominee hearing

The Democratic staffer told reporters that because the committee did not adopt rules at the beginning of the 119th Congress, it has been operating under rules from the 118th, which required the attendance of at least one member of the minority party to constitute a quorum for reporting bills or nominations.

“The remaining recourse is to basically go to the floor and . . . make an inquiry in terms of what took place today, and then there would have to be a formal ruling by the chair,” they said.

They added that in determining whether the committee had a quorum to advance the nomination, “It would depend on how they view our committee rules from the 118th that we practice under for the 119th versus what the Senate rules are.” The staffer said they have not yet spoken with committee Democrats or Democratic leadership about plans for such an inquiry.

Democrats also previously boycotted a committee markup in March over an aviation safety bill left off the committee’s agenda, after which action was deferred. The committee later came to agreement and rescheduled the markup.

In their letter Monday, Democrats quoted Cruz from a 2014 statement about the nomination of Loretta Lynch to be attorney general.

“As you wrote in 2014, controversial nominees ‘should not be confirmed in the lame duck session of Congress by senators who just lost their seats and are no longer accountable to the voters.’ We agree,” the letter said.

On Tuesday, Sen. Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., wrote his own letter to Cruz calling for the removal of the nomination from the agenda based on grounds that Thumann Severs lied to the committee.

“While Ms. Thumann testified she did not work ‘on any media-related issues,’ documents obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests demonstrate that she worked on several media related issues, including on commitments that Skydance made to pave the way for FCC approval of its merger with Paramount,” Luján wrote.

Democrats have criticized the FCC and Carr for allowing media consolidation, including by Skydance. There has also been bipartisan criticism of Carr’s threats against broadcasters for speech he disagrees with.

Luján told reporters Wednesday prior to the markup that he expects, under Democratic control next year, Carr and potentially Thumann Severs would be called to testify.

“I have questions. I certainly hope that Brendan Carr will voluntarily show up to this committee when invited, and that other rules and tools do not need to be used,” Luján said, responding to a question about possibly subpoenaing Carr. “But . . . everything should be on the table.”

Sen. Jerry Moran, R-Kan., said at the markup that he spoke with Thumann Severs about her role at the FCC and her “lack of engagement” as the commission has made decisions regarding broadcasters. He also said he found her testimony at last week’s nomination hearing “comforting.”

“I have concerns with FCC action in regard to political speech, broadcasters, and she indicated in her answers . . . in a way that provided me with a level of comfort about her nomination in regard to that issue,” Moran said.

Moran also said he hopes to meet with Thumann Severs before her nomination is brought to the floor.

#6193. Wry and Wistful Landscapes at Kansas City’s Splendid Nelson-Atkins Museum

The museum needs to ditch its proposed expansion, an unneeded temple to therapy culture.

Joel Sternfeld, McLean, Virginia, December 4, 1978, printed 2005, dye transfer print.

The Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art, © Joel Sternfeld

‘E verything’s Up to Date in Kansas City” — that few minutes of pure effervescence in Oklahoma refers to Kansas City circa 1907, when it was in the middle of its version of the City Beautiful movement. New boulevards, new, fancy neighborhoods, hundreds of fountains, and much more were in the works. The sparkle of a new art museum was in the civic eye, too. The Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art didn’t open its doors until 1933, but better late than never. It’s an essential visit for art lovers.

I visited last month and saw the very enjoyable exhibition American Prospects and Landscape Photography, 1839 to Today. It presents Joel Sternfeld’s lovely, often sad, wry, late-1970s and early-1980s landscape photographs in the context of the American landscape-photography genre. I love Sternfeld’s work. Born in 1944, he was the cutting-edge photographer who took color landscape photography mainstream, mostly through American Prospects, his portfolio of photographs published in book form in 1987. Color? Cutting-edge in the ’80s? Well, 1987 is about to be 40 years ago, so it qualifies as days of yore, and what has became American Prospects started in the late ’70s, when Sternfeld started an epic road trip to make art about Americans and the land. Landscape photography was, à la Ansel Adams, commonly in black and white, thought to evoke grandeur and mystery. What pushed Sternfeld to color was the advent of Kodak Vericolor III film in the 1970s. It delivered accurate, vibrant color and was good for various lighting and especially skin tones.

Brian T. Allen is National Review’s art critic.

On “Wry and Wistful Landscapes at Kansas City’s Splendid Nelson-Atkins Museum”

#6192. Most Airports Cap Concession Prices… But The System Is A Total Joke

Travelers are conditioned to expect high prices at airport retailers and restaurants, so over $5 for a bottle of water at an airport shop, or $25 for a burger at a mediocre airport restaurant, might not catch anyone off guard.

However, did you know there are caps on how much retailers at airports are supposed to be able to charge, and they’re largely just not enforced? Well, or perhaps more accurately, they are enforced, but using very dishonest math. The backstory of this is interesting.

Airports generate revenue in a variety of ways, and one of the major ways is through the retailers they have in the terminal. An airport is like a shopping mall with a very captive audience, and as you’d expect, rent for businesses in airports is absolutely through the roof, as a result of that.

But in order to balance things out and prevent retailers from exploiting consumers, over 80% of airports in the United States specifically stipulate the maximum prices that airports can charge consumers. These terms are typically baked into the contracts that airport retailers sign, and failure to adhere to the rules can lead to consequences, at least in theory.

The airports with pricing caps for airport businesses generally fall into one of two categories:

If there are supposed to be rules in place capping airport pricing, then why is this such a widespread issue? More Perfect Union recently published a great video investigating this issue, and it’s a fascinating watch. First they actually analyze airport pricing, and then they confront airport authorities about the lack of enforcement.

Here’s what’s interesting — airport retailers do have to submit comparisons for benchmark pricing, to prove that they’re not violating rules and exploiting customers. The issue is what kind of businesses are considered comparable for the purposes of “street pricing.”

For example, 9NEWS recently investigated this at Denver Airport, finding that a basic Starbucks coffee cost $4.55 in the airport, compared to $2.95 outside the airport (a 54% markup), and a bag of cashews cost $9.99 in the airport, compared to $4.74 outside the airport (a 110% markup).

The airport’s VP of Concessions agreed to sit down with the reporter to discuss this, and she said the results of his investigation were great news — she suggested that 93% of the prices were compliant, and said “that’s pretty darn good.” How could that be, given the high markups compared to nearby businesses?

The issue boils down to how much latitude businesses have to submit pricing comparisons:

What’s wild is how the airport official responds to Starbucks just having consistent pricing, and violating the rules:

VP of Concessions: “What I get from that is, they’re looking for consistency, across the board, across the nation, across the world.”Reporter: “I can’t help but think that travelers may be looking for consistency, but if they see a cheaper cup of coffee, they’ll probably be okay with it.”VP of Concessions: “I don’t know the answer to that. This is how we take care of our passengers, by ensuring that they are paying fair and transparent pricing, while supporting our business partners.”

Back to the original story, the More Perfect Union reporter confronted the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey about pricing like $6.89 for one liter of Smart Water, compared to closer to $3.50 at nearby bodegas.

The response was that “comparing a Hudson to a bodega isn’t appropriate,” because “Hudson is a specialty market.” The approved price comparison was reportedly based on the price of water at Tablet Works, a “wellness & concierge pharmacy” in a high-end mall.

The other thing to keep in mind is that a large percentage of airport retailers and restaurants are run by the same few companies, like HMSHost, which is a subsidiary of Avolta. So clearly they have a centralized approach to submitting pricing comparisons, and know exactly what they’re doing. Interestingly, the few independent businesses in some airports were found to have the most honest pricing.

So to sum it up, the system is designed to be rigged. Airport authorities can technically pretend they’re looking out for consumers by setting a cap. Retailers can submit pricing comparisons to the highest prices they can find anywhere. Then airport authorities verify those prices to pretend they’re doing their jobs.

Airports are obviously complicit in all of this. They make money by charging sky high rent, and the reason they can do that is because retailers can charge hugely inflated prices. The more profits retailers make, the more airports can charge in rent. And they know that no consumer is going to avoid an airport because of high concession costs.

Around 80% of airports in the United States cap the prices that retailers can charge, so in most cases, you’re not supposed to be paying more than 15% above “street pricing.” The issue is the liberties that businesses can take with what constitutes “street pricing.”

The price of the bottle of water or smoothie you’re buying isn’t compared to what you’d pay at a nearby gas station and smoothie shop, but instead, is being compared to what you’d pay at Erewhon. Talk about a very broken system, with no incentives for any party to actually be honest…

What do you make of this airport pricing situation?

#6191. Emirates Finally Revamping Dubai Lounges: Temporary New First Class Lounge Now Open

Emirates is known for being a world-class airline, though at this point, the carrier’s ground experience at Dubai International Airport (DXB) leaves a lot to be desired, especially for premium passengers.

While I don’t want to suggest that the carrier’s first class lounges and business class lounges are terrible, they’re far from cutting edge, and the design definitely feels extremely outdated. Earlier this year, I wrote a post asking if Emirates was going to revamp its lounges at the airport, or just wait until the theoretical move to Dubai World Central (DWC) around 2032.

Well, it seems that my concerns have now been addressed, as Emirates has announced plans to completely transform its lounge experience in Dubai. Over the summer we saw the airline start to roll out a new global lounge concept for outstation lounges, and that idea is now coming to Dubai as well.

As is the case for any airline, rolling out a new lounge concept at a hub airport isn’t easy, given that it requires spaces to be closed. So that’s why it’s worth noting that Emirates is taking an innovative approach to refreshing its lounges in Dubai:

Emirates is investing a total of 400 million AED ($109 million) in these lounge spaces. Interestingly, Emirates claims that “all flagship lounges” will be getting a redesign, though there’s zero mention of the lounges in Concourse A, which are the biggest lounges in the world (they span the entire concourse), and offer direct boarding to planes. So it’s not clear when those lounges will undergo updates.

Here’s how Emirates President Tim Clark describes this development:

“Our customers expect the very best from Emirates, whether while flying or spending time with us on the ground. We believe the airport experience should be every bit as exceptional as the journey itself, and that’s why we are transforming our lounges globally. This new First Class Lounge in Dubai is the first taste of what’s to come. And if these are the lengths we will go to for a temporary lounge… just imagine what you can expect from new Emirates Lounges going forward. Over the next two years, we’ll be unveiling a completely different lounge experience, with new concepts in dining, wellness, entertainment and personalised hospitality. We’re going well beyond a traditional refurbishment and creating extraordinary spaces.”

We’ve already seen how Emirates is overhauling its global lounge network, and I’d say the changes are pretty awesome. So what can we expect in Dubai? As you can see, Clark references how the temporary new first class lounge is just a small glimpse into what we can expect in the future. Below is a video showing the new concept, and I must say, it looks impressive!

Here’s how Emirates describes the lounge concept, broadly:

Featuring immersive culinary experiences to dedicated wellness facilities and innovative entertainment concepts, Emirates is redefining what customers can expect from their time at the airport. Building on Emirates’ renowned hospitality, customers can expect distinct spaces for dining, relaxation, work and socialising – complemented by intuitive technology, refined interiors and elevated personal service. Each lounge will bear the hallmarks of the iconic Emirates brand, with the interiors conveying luxury, comfort, exceptional hospitality and global appeal.

When it comes to the temporary new first class lounge, here are the details:

As much as people like to suggest that Gulf carriers just throw money down the drain when it comes to passenger experience, Emirates is actually a pretty disciplined and cost focused business, which is also clear based on the fact that the airline still has angled business class seats with seven seats per row. 😉

But when the airline does invest and upgrade its products, it has a pretty good sense of what customers like. Barista coffee, Dom Perignon, and a gym? Count me in (though maybe the amenities shouldn’t be enjoyed in that order). 😉 It does sound like there still won’t be dedicated bedrooms, which would be disappointing, but also wouldn’t surprise me, given the volume of rooms they’d need to serve guests.

Emirates is hugely investing in its lounge network in Dubai, something that’s long overdue, if you ask me. Over the next two years, at least four lounges will be getting a full makeover, to match the carrier’s new lounge aesthetic.

We’ve just seen the opening of a new temporarily first class lounge in Concourse B, which is described as an example of what’s to come. Next year that lounge is expected to become a business class lounge, as a new flagship first class lounge opens, along with additional first and business class lounges.

The new design aesthetic looks great, and it sounds like some thought is being put into amenities as well. I look forward to seeing this transformation, though I can’t help but wonder if this reflects a delay with Emirates moving to its new hub airport.

What do you make of Emirates’ new lounge concept?

#6189. FAA Technician Only Unlocked The Door: Inside The Oversight Gap Behind The Nationwide Ground Stop

Last Friday we saw the worst disruption to air travel that we’ve seen in the United States in over 25 years, as air traffic shut down nationwide for over four hours. We quickly learned that this happened because L3Harris, a government contractor, was doing maintenance to switch telecommunications lines from copper to fiber.

The logical question is how something going wrong with the work of one contractor could cause our entire aviation ecosystem to shut down:

So, what’s actually going on here? A new report sheds some more light on this…

CNN has some insights into how little oversight there was of the work being performed by FAA contractor L3Harris, which led to the ground stop disaster that we saw. When was oversight reduced? Well, in early 2025, coinciding with the FAA laying off a large number of employees, as part of Elon Musk’s “Department of Government Efficiency” (DOGE) stunt.

According to this report, last Friday morning, an FAA technician escorted a contractor from L3Harris into a remote radio communications site for air traffic control in southern Arkansas, to replace a decades-old router. The FAA technician’s belief was that his role was done once the contractor entered the facility, according to people familiar with what happened, plus the union representing FAA employees.

That router replacement ended up being what triggered the communications issues across the country, ultimately leading to the nationwide ground stop.

FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford insists that the L3Harris engineer performing the upgrade “was monitored by an FAA technician” and that a risk assessment was performed, but sources dispute that characterization, pointing out that the technician “was only there to unlock the door,” and that “there was no monitoring.”

Funny enough, an FAA spokesperson later contradicted Bedford, saying “the FAA escort is responsible for providing the L3Harris technician access to and from the building,” and “because it is L3 equipment, the escort is not there while the technician is doing work.” It’s amazing how they can’t even keep their narrative straight.

This type of hands-off arrangement is apparently a recent development that happened under the Trump administration, and a change to how the FAA used to handle things. In March 2025, an FAA memo laid out changes to how FAA maintenance and upgrades would be carried out, in order to speed things up. The memo stated that “it is critical to approve maintenance performed by the Telecommunication Vendors without delay.”

With this policy, the FAA also went from receiving maintenance “requests” from private contractors that needed to be approved, to receiving “notifications” of intended work, noting that “this work will proceed without FAA approval,” if not processed in time.

While the memo claimed that an FAA liaison will evaluate the “purpose, severity, criticality and impact” of the work, there are reportedly only a handful of liaisons nationwide, processing thousands of notifications. In this case, L3Harris reportedly submitted its “notification” with just a few days notice, meaning there was no meaningful oversight.

A spokesperson for the union representing FAA employees explains that “orders were to simply let the contractor in the building,” that he “had no direction to help or assist in any way,” and that “no PASS-represented employee was asked to conduct a risk assessment on this particular upgrade.”

DUFFY: How many times does this have to happen before congress gives the money to fix it?R: You’ve been in office almost two years now, Republicans controlled both chambers of congress and still do.DUFFY: What your network are you from? pic.twitter.com/xuX5arTwjl

It also has to be pointed out that the March 2025 memo about a reduction in oversight came just weeks after Elon Musk’s DOGE laid off hundreds of FAA employees, making for the biggest single year layoffs at the organization in history.

That’s the beauty of slashing government inefficiency, right? If everything is working well, then we must not need all of those employees, eh? So to have a handful of people being “notified” of work and having to do an analysis sounds like it could be a problem.

We have to be honest, in general, politicians are really bad at accountability, and being honest when things go wrong. But whether you like Trump’s policies or not, there’s no denying that he takes lack of accountability to new levels. Everything good that happens is immediately his doing, and everything bad is Biden’s fault.

It would be nice if one Trump administration official actually had the introspection to say “hey, let’s make sure this doesn’t happen again,” rather than just yelling “give me $50 billion” and “Biden, Buttigieg, Biden, Buttigieg.”

We’re getting a clearer picture of the circumstances that caused the nationwide ground stop last Friday, the biggest disruption to US air travel since 9/11. A contractor with L3Harris was given access to a site to replace wiring, with virtually no oversight from an FAA employee.

While the FAA claims that there’s supposed to be oversight of contractor work, in this case the FAA employee was reportedly just tasked with unlocking the door. The approach to overseeing contractor work is reportedly a new system as of March 2025, where contractor work went from being viewed as “requests” to being viewed as “notifications,” with just a handful of people to oversee these requests. This came just weeks after hundreds of employees were laid off from the FAA, thanks to Musk’s DOGE.

What do you make of this FAA contractor oversight situation?

#6187. Atmos Rewards Business Card Changes: Higher(ish) Fee, New Benefits

Atmos Rewards is the loyalty program of Alaska and Hawaiian, and that includes three co-branded credit cards. There’s only one business credit card in the portfolio, and that’s the Atmos™ Rewards Visa Signature® Business Card.

Along those lines, there’s a major update, as the card has just undergone a full refresh. The bad news is that the card’s annual fee has gone up considerably (at least for most people), and the benefits have also changed. Let’s take a look, because as you’d expect, the changes are a mixed bag.

The good news is that there’s a huge incentive to apply for the card, given the massive limited-time welcome bonus of 90,000 Atmos Rewards points after spending $6,000 within the first 90 days.

Link: Learn more about the Atmos™ Rewards Visa Signature® Business Card

The Atmos Rewards Business Card is undergoing some major updates. This includes a higher annual fee, new rewards structure, and new set of perks. However, these changes only apply to new card members, as existing card members will keep the old benefits (and fee).

Let me emphasize that the card has a huge limited time welcome bonus of 90,000 Atmos Rewards points after spending $6,000 within the first 90 days. So that’s a major incentive to apply for the card, if you’re eligible. I value Atmos Rewards points at 1.5 cents each, so to me, that’s worth $1,350.

With that out of the way, let’s go over the details…

The Atmos Rewards Business Card now has a flat $195 annual fee, which covers the primary card member and any employee cards. Previously, the card had an annual fee of $70 per company, plus $25 per employee, so the minimum annual fee you’d pay would be $95.

It goes without saying that this change represents a significant increase in the annual fee, unless you had more than four employee credit cards on your account.

The Atmos Rewards Business Card also has a new rewards structure. The card now offers:

What has changed here is the new 10x points for booking through Atmos for Business (great for those who can use it), as well as a full overhaul of the 2x points categories. Previously the card offered 2x points on eligible gas, EV charging stations, shipping, and local transit purchases (including rideshare), while now it just offers 2x points on dining. As before, the card offers one status point for every $3 spent, with no cap.

The Atmos Rewards Business Card is picking up quite a few new benefits that it didn’t previously offer:

The refreshed card also keeps a first checked bag free and preferred boarding on Alaska and Hawaiian flights for the card member and up to six guests on the same reservation when the trip is paid with the card, a 20% rebate on eligible inflight purchases, a 10% rewards bonus for cardholders with an eligible Bank of America small business account, and no foreign transaction fees.

Let me emphasize that the card will no longer offer a $99 companion fare, so that’s being replaced by the new 50% off vouchers that can be earned with spending.

As of November 18, 2026, customers who apply for a new Atmos Rewards Business Card will be receiving the refreshed card, with the new benefits and fee.

Applications submitted before November 18 will continue under the prior card offering. What’s interesting is that current cardholders will keep their existing benefits, and will not be automatically moved over. However, you can call up Bank of America if you’d like to see about the opportunity of switching.

As of now, it sounds like there are no plans to transition people to the new system, so existing card members shouldn’t be negatively impacted by this.

The Atmos Rewards Business Card changes are a mixed bag. First, I want to once again emphasize that since existing card members aren’t impacted by these changes, I don’t think there should be too much frustration here.

In the past, the Atmos Rewards Business Card basically felt like the business version of the $95 annual fee Atmos™ Rewards Ascent Visa Signature® credit card (learn more), while now the card feels more like a hybrid between that and the $395 annual fee Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® Credit Card (learn more), in terms of both cost and benefits.

Admittedly it’s hard to do an apples-to-apples comparison between personal and business cards, because at least in theory, they’re supposed to serve different purposes. So here’s my take:

So I don’t have a terribly strong take here, other than wishing that spending on the card were a bit more lucrative, and more competitive with what’s offered by the Atmos Rewards Summit Card. The Summit Card will continue to be my go-to card for Atmos Rewards.

The Atmos Rewards Business Card has just undergone some major changes, though they don’t impact existing card members. For new applicants, the card now has a $195 annual fee, compared to the old fee of $70 for the company, and $25 per person.

The card is also getting a new set of benefits, including a new rewards structure, additional perks, and new incentives for spending. People will have varying takes as to whether these changes are positive or negative, depending on their consumer patterns.

My biggest takeaway is that the bonus of 90,000 Atmos Rewards points upon completing minimum spending is excellent, and a great incentive to apply for the card.

What do you make of these Atmos Rewards Business Card changes?

#6186. Sanders: ‘Medicare for All’ will be HELP priority

Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., holds a news conference in the Capitol on Nov. 10. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Saying that “Medicare for All” is no longer “a radical idea,” Sen. Bernie Sanders said Wednesday that he would prioritize passing the universal health care plan if he assumes the chairmanship of the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee next year as expected.

Democrats could bring it about through the filibuster-proof budget reconciliation process, the Vermont independent and avowed democratic socialist told reporters. And the idea could be buoyed by an influx of progressive lawmakers elected in the midterms.

Sanders said Medicare for All is gaining support from voters across the country who are looking to overhaul the American health care system as costs have soared. Democrats on the committee will move the legislation “as aggressively as we can, as rapidly as we can,” he said.

His version, introduced in April and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, would implement the universal health care system over four years. In the first year, the the age of Medicare eligibility would drop to 55 from 65, while coverage would expand to include dental, hearing and vision care. The bill would also provide coverage for eligible children during the first year.

The age of eligibility would fall another 10 years in each of the following years until the fourth year, when coverage would be extended to all Americans.

“If there has ever been a time in the modern history of our country . . . to address the crises facing working families, this is that time,” Sanders said, noting that Democrats will have a 56-44 majority when the 120th Congress begins in January, the largest margin for either party in 16 years.

Sen. Tammy Baldwin, D-Wis., along with nine other Senate Democrats, last week offered an alternative Medicare expansion plan, which would lower the eligibility to those ages 50 and up.

While who will be leading Senate Democrats is still an open question — Chris Van Hollen of Maryland is challenging Charles E. Schumer of New York, who has been the top Senate Democrat since 2017 — Sanders said he is confident the Medicare for All bill will get to the Senate floor, “no matter who the [Senate majority] leader is.” Sanders previously expressed opposition to Schumer leading the conference.

Asked about efforts to extend the Affordable Care Act enhanced subsidies, Sanders responded he’s “all in.” However, he added “the American people and elected officials understand the current health care system is broken.”

Subsidies that help enrollees pay for health care premiums on the ACA exchanges were expanded during the COVID-19 pandemic, but these enhanced credits expired at the end of last year, raising costs for many who relied on them to help defray costs.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, nominated on Wednesday to be speaker next year, previously outlined broader health care priorities such as extending the ACA tax credits and reversing Medicaid cuts enacted in Republicans' reconciliation package last year. When asked Tuesday how far Democrats want to lower the Medicare eligibility age, Jeffries responded, “that’s all part of an ongoing conversation.”

In addition to expanding Medicare coverage, Sanders reiterated his push to lower prescription drug prices. The Vermont lawmaker previously introduced legislation aimed at reducing the cost of brand name prescription drugs by linking domestic prices to international price benchmarks.

To enact some of the agenda, Sanders may have to court Republicans.

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., said last week that he plans to serve as the top Republican on the HELP committee next year. Sanders said Wednesday that his likely GOP counterpart “has shown an enormous amount of courage in taking on Republican leadership year after year.”

Sanders added that although Paul may have a different viewpoint from himself on committee issues, he looks forward to finding common ground.

#6185. Buy Air Canada Aeroplan Points With 100% Bonus (1.31 Cents Each): Worth It?

The Air Canada Aeroplan program is currently offering a bonus on purchased points. While this is a mystery bonus, where different members may be eligible for different offers, it seems the best version is for up to a 100% bonus.

Is there value with this offer? With a specific use in mind, absolutely, in my opinion. Aeroplan is one of my all-around favorite frequent flyer programs, thanks to the huge variety of airline partners, the ability to have stopovers on one-way awards for 5,000 points, and the generally great online booking experience.

Link: Buy Air Canada Aeroplan points with this promotion with up to a 100% bonus

Between 12AM PT on November 19 and 11:50PM PT on December 10, 2026, the Air Canada Aeroplan program is offering a promotion on purchased points.

Different members may be eligible for different offers, so you’ll want to log into your account to see what you’re eligible for. However, it appears that the best version of the offer is for up to a 100% bonus, structured as follows:

I should emphasize that other members seem to be eligible for offers of 85%, 90%, or 95%, so it’s no guarantee that everyone will see the 100% offer.

Ordinarily, Air Canada Aeroplan charges $0.0375 CAD (~0.026 USD) per point. Any purchases made with US credit cards and US billing addresses aren’t subject to sales tax either.

If you purchased 500,000 Aeroplan points with a 100% bonus, you’d receive a total of 1,000,000 Aeroplan points at a cost of $18,750 CAD (~$13,101 USD), which is a rate of 1.31 cents (USD) per Aeroplan point.

If you wanted to purchase the fewest possible points at the best possible price, you’d want to buy exactly 90,000 points at a cost of $3,375 CAD (~$2,358 USD), which would potentially get you 180,000 points, for the same cost per point.

While you can purchase up to one million Aeroplan points per account per calendar year, there’s ordinarily a per-transaction limit of 250,000 points pre-bonus. However, during this promotion that has been doubled, to 500,000 points.

Aeroplan points purchases typically post pretty close to instantly, though in some situations, it could take up to 72 hours for points to post. Note that the purchase of Aeroplan points is non-refundable, and Aeroplan points purchases also don’t count toward elite status.

When Air Canada Aeroplan offer a promotion on purchased points, we most commonly see a bonus in the range of 90-110%, but the exact offers do vary. Personally I’d buy points based on when you’re ready to redeem them, rather than the exact cost. After all, the cost to buy points with a 100% bonus vs. a 110% bonus isn’t vastly different.

Below is a chart with some of the recent promotions we saw from the Aeroplan program, before this one.

Air Canada Aeroplan points purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as an airfare purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. Therefore I’d recommend using a card on which you’re trying to reach a minimum spending requirement, or otherwise, a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending.

Since the purchase of Aeroplan points is billed in CAD, there is one other great option. The Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® Credit Card (learn more) offers 3x points on foreign purchases, so that’s a fantastic card for this kind of purchase. Beyond that, the best options would be cards that offer 2x transferable points, while having no foreign transaction fees.

Aeroplan is one of my favorite frequent flyer programs out there. To cover a few of the basics:

There are lots of phenomenal uses of Aeroplan points, and this is a program that I redeem through regularly. Just keep in mind that Aeroplan now has dynamic award pricing on select partners, including Emirates, Etihad, FlyDubai, and United, among others.

One of my favorite things about Air Canada Aeroplan is that the program has more airline partners than any other frequent flyer program, and you can redeem points on over 45 airlines. In addition to Air Canada belonging to the Star Alliance, Aeroplan also partners with airlines that include Etihad, Azul, Air Serbia, Virgin Australia, Air Dolomiti, Eurowings, Gulf Air, Oman Air, Air Mauritius, and Emirates.

Always look up award availability before buying points, to get a sense of what you can expect.

Many consumers are frustrated by the practice of airlines adding carrier imposed surcharges to award tickets. In the case of Aeroplan, there are no fuel surcharges on award tickets, meaning you shouldn’t expect to pay big fees when redeeming points.

Everyone will value points currencies differently. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Aeroplan points to be worth 1.4 cents each. However, I tend to value points pretty conservatively, and there are many ways to get way more value from Aeroplan points than that.

Air Canada Aeroplan points only expire after 18 months of inactivity. However, any account activity that leads to earning or redeeming points (including buying them) would reset the expiration.

While buying Aeroplan points could represent a great deal, keep in mind that there are lots of other ways to earn Aeroplan points. Most significantly, Aeroplan is transfer partners with American Express Membership Rewards, Bilt Rewards, Capital One, and Chase Ultimate Rewards, making the currency pretty easy to acquire. From all those currencies, rewards transfer at a 1:1 ratio, and sometimes you’ll even find transfer bonuses.

On top of that, in the United States there’s the Chase Air Canada Aeroplan® Credit Card (learn more), which is pretty lucrative.

Air Canada’s Aeroplan program is offering a bonus on purchased points. While people may be targeted for different offers, it appears the best offer is for up to a 100% bonus, which kicks in as long as you purchase at least 90,000 points in one transaction. This is an opportunity to buy points for 1.31 cents (in USD) each.

This could represent a good deal, and there are plenty of situations under which the math will work out for this promotion. Still, in general I’d only recommend buying points with a short term use in mind, as there’s always risk to holding onto points for longer periods of time.

I am seeing this movie star, yet I checked both hands and I am not in possession of popcorn, nor am I in a supine position on my couch. Something is way off here.

It was even more confusing in July 2024 when I (quite literally) almost bumped into the notorious comedian Russell Brand at the Republican National Convention in Milwaukee. I turned a corner, and there he was, the three-time recipient of The Sun’s “Shagger of the Year” award in the flesh, working the convention and interviewing GOP stars for his online show.

Russell Brand arrives at Southwark Crown Court during the fourth week of his trial on charges of rape and sexual assault, in London, England, November 3, 2026.

Christian Schneider is a National Review contributor and writes the Anti-Knowledge newsletter. He is a co-host of the podcast Wasn't That Special: 50 Years of SNL.

#6182. Alaska Atmos Rewards Business Card Bonus: 90K Points Welcome Offer

The $195 annual fee Atmos™ Rewards Visa Signature® Business Card currently has a huge bonus of 90,000 Atmos Rewards points after spending $6,000 within the first 90 days. For context, this is the business card of the Atmos Rewards portfolio, the loyalty program of Alaska and Hawaiian. This is a potentially lucrative card that has just undergone a refresh, and you can read my Atmos Rewards Business Card review here.

In this post I’d like to go over the details of the Atmos Rewards Business Card bonus, for anyone who may be considering applying. There are lots of reasons to get this card, particularly the incredible bonus.

Link: Learn more about the Atmos™ Rewards Visa Signature® Business Card with 90K bonus points

The Atmos Rewards Business Card currently has a welcome offer of 90,000 Atmos Rewards bonus points after spending $6,000 within the first 90 days.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Atmos Rewards points to be worth 1.5 cents each, meaning the 90,000 points are worth $1,350 to me, which is among the best bonuses out there. There are lots of great uses of Atmos Rewards points, for travel on Alaska, Hawaiian, oneworld partners, and non-alliance partners.

Atmos Rewards points have all kinds of uses, ranging from booking short haul one-way economy awards on American for 4,500 points, to booking Starlux business class one-way awards from the US to Asia for 75,000 points. Of course capacity controls apply, so patience and flexibility will be required to get the best deal. Still, I find this to be one of the most useful points currencies out there.

The Atmos Rewards Business Card 90,000-point offer is the best publicly available sign-up bonus that we’ve seen on the card since it launched in August 2025 (which is when the Atmos Rewards program formally launched). How do the previous Atmos Rewards Business Card bonuses compare?

As you can see, the Atmos Rewards Business Card sign-up bonus has varied from 70,000 points to 90,000 points, and the current bonus of 90,000 points is the best publicly available offer we’ve seen. So if there has ever been a time to apply for this card, this is it.

When it comes to getting approved for the Atmos Rewards Business Card, what rules should you be aware of? There are the card specific policies, and then also the more generic Bank of America policies. When you pull up the application, you’ll see the following terms:

This one-time promotion is limited to company level Business Card clients opening a new account in response to this offer and will not apply to requests to convert existing accounts.

The good news is that eligibility for the Atmos Rewards Business Card is considered completely independently of any other cards in the portfolio, so you’re eligible if you have either of the personal Atmos Rewards credit cards. Many people even report being eligible for the Atmos Rewards Business Card (including the bonus) if they’ve had it in the past.

Beyond that, Bank of America doesn’t have many consistent restrictions when it comes to getting approved for business cards. While Bank of America has the 2/3/4 rule and 3/12 rules, those apply to personal cards, and not business cards. Generally those with a Bank of America banking relationship also have the best odds of approval (though it’s by no means a requirement).

There’s not a consistent credit score you need to have to be approved for this card, though personally I’d hope to have a score in the “good” to “excellent” range, ideally 700+ points. However, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected.

Applying for this card won’t count as a further card toward Chase’s 5/24 rule, in case that’s a limit you’re trying to stay under.

Beyond the great bonus, there are multiple reasons to consider the $195 annual fee Atmos Rewards Business Card:

If you fly Alaska or Hawaiian with any frequency, then having this card should be a no-brainer. The benefits really add up, between the lounge passes, the first checked bag free, preferred boarding, savings on inflight purchases, and more.

The Atmos Rewards Business Card has introduced a best-ever welcome offer, whereby you can earn 90,000 Atmos Rewards points upon completing minimum spending.

This is an exceptional bonus, and this card is absolutely worth picking up for the points, especially given that eligibility isn’t mutually exclusive with other Atmos Rewards cards. In the long run, the card can be worth it for the perks for travel on Alaska and Hawaiian.

Anecdotally I find Bank of America business cards to be quite easy to get approved for, including if you’ve had the card in the past. Applying for this card also shouldn’t count as a further card toward the Chase 5/24 limit, if that’s of concern to you.

Anyone plan to pick up the Atmos Rewards Business Card with this great offer?

#6181. Finnair Celebrates International Men’s Day With All-Male Crew On Flight

There’s still quite a gender gap in the airline industry, with a disproportionate number of pilots being male, and a disproportionate number of flight attendants being female. Airlines will sometimes have special celebrations with all-female crews, so here’s an interesting twist on that.

Today is (apparently) International Men’s Day. We often see airlines commemorate International Women’s Day, but there aren’t many airlines that celebrate the equivalent for men… well, except Finnair! The airline has today operated its annual flight with an all-male crew. This was the case for Finnair flight AY1331, from Helsinki (HEL) to London (LHR), using an Airbus A350-900.

The crew consisted of 10 people, comprised of two pilots and eight flight attendants. The gate agents were also all men. So, why is this important? Finnair highlights how only around 10% of cabin crew at the airline are male, but the company hopes to see that number grow in the future.

I think this is a fun concept, and it would be nice to see a closer to 50/50 gender ratio in both the cockpit and cabin, as it would show that everyone is given a fair chance at such a career.

I think it’s worth acknowledging that at many airlines, hiring of flight attendants is still primarily or exclusively based on gender. Now, the policies do vary significantly by airline, but perhaps an extreme example is India’s largest airline, IndiGo, which only hires female flight attendants. It’s literally written on the application, that it’s a job for “Female Indian nationals.”

It’s all so strange, because the airline has this super enthusiastic page about the importance of diversity in the workplace, and says “all employment decisions are made solely on the basis of merit and qualifications, without regard to a candidate’s gender…” You mean except the single largest portion of your workforce, which is cabin crew?

What’s interesting is that while those gender restrictions exist in the cabin, roughly 18% of the carrier’s pilots are female, which is way above the global average of 7%. That’s obviously a conscious effort, so I guess the idea is that women can become pilots but men can’t become flight attendants.

In fairness, I suspect part of the motivation here is that IndiGo flight attendants share hotel rooms on layovers, and that is a bit more complicated with mixed genders. Then again, it seems easy enough to just try to pair male flight attendants on trips, so it’s hardly a hurdle that can’t be overcome.

While we’re used to seeing airlines celebrate International Women’s Day, it’s rare to see an airline celebrating International Men’s Day. Finnair has operated an all-male flight today, intended to highlight how only 10% of flight attendants at the airline are male, and the airline wants to change that. While an unconventional initiative nowadays, I think this is still pretty cool.

What do you make of Finnair’s all-male flight?

#6179. Amex Auto-Enrolling Card Members In Paperless Billing (Sorry, Dad!)

Dad, here’s a blog post you should pay attention to (and thanks to Steve for flagging this)…

With banks, it’s typically possible to get your account statements by email or mail. There’s no denying that consumer preferences have shifted over the years, and along those lines, Amex has just sent an email to card members, informing them that “we’re making the switch to paperless.” Here’s the main part of the email:

We’re making the switch to paperless billing statements and account communications, beginning February 2027.

Here’s what happens nextWe want to help you get ready to make the switch too. So, we’ve enrolled your account listed above in the paperless delivery option – but for now, we’ll continue to send you communications about your account in the mail. We’ll also mail your billing statements for the closing dates of November 2026, December 2026, and January 2027.

After that, we’ll send account communications to you by email, and you’ll receive your monthly billing statements electronically. When they’re ready, you’ll be able to view them anytime by logging in to your account online at americanexpress.com or in the American Express App.

Now, that makes it sound like people will be forced to switch to paperless billing, but I don’t believe that’s actually the case? Because further down in the email, it says this:

Not ready to go paperless? No problem! You can re-enroll in paper billing statements and account communications by going to americanexpress.com/paperlesssettings, selecting “U.S. Mail,” and following the prompts to opt back in.

So it seems like what’s happening here is that Amex will try to force everyone into paperless billing by making it the default, but maybe those who specifically once again state their preferences for paper billing will be able to maintain that communication method?

Suffice it to say that going back 25 years, a vast majority of people got paper statements for their credit cards, while nowadays a vast majority of people get paperless statements, obviously reflecting the shift we’ve seen in how the internet is used.

It’s funny, because I’m sure 99% of OMAAT readers would be confused at the thought of getting paper bills, and would wonder what purpose that serves. But then there are also people like my dad, who rely on paper statements for their credit cards, pay their statement by phone, etc.

So it does sound like people will have the option of opting back into paper billing after being auto-enrolled in paperless billing, so the concept isn’t being eliminated altogether. Still, for my dad, there would likely be quite the learning curve.

Then again, up until less than a decade ago he didn’t have a cell phone and insisted he didn’t need one, while now he kind of loves it, for everything from texting, to Googling all kinds of stuff. That’s of course a double-edged sword as well, because he seems to believe that if the Google AI summary says something, it must be true. We’re not talking things like vaccines. Instead, we’re talking things like whether the salmon at Red Lobster is good, etc. Anyway, I digress…

As of February 2027, Amex will be automatically moving those with paper billing to paperless billing. While the message makes it sound like people will be forced to switch to paperless billing, that doesn’t seem to be the case, as Amex is also telling people they can once again enroll in paper billing statements and account communications if they’re “not ready to go paperless.” So Amex just seems to be trying to thin the ranks here of those using this feature.

What do you make of Amex’s switch to paperless billing?

#6178. Aeromexico 787s Get Makeover With New Business Class, Premium Economy

Aeromexico is planning some major upgrades to its wide body fleet, which consists exclusively of Boeing 787s. This is interesting on many levels — we’ll see the larger Dreamliners get all-new business class cabins plus premium economy for the first time, we’ll see the smaller Dreamliners get the old business class cabins of the bigger Dreamliners, and we’ll see the airline adopt some Delta-style branding.

To start, let me provide the context that Aeromexico’s Boeing 787 fleet currently consists of 25 planes, including:

Aeromexico is planning on fully overhauling the premium cabins on these planes, as was announced by the company’s CEO at this week’s APEX FTE EXPO 2026.

The plan is for the 787-9s to get all-new cabins, and in the process, the 787-8s will get the old business class seats from the 787-9s. That means the 787-8s will get reverse herringbone seats, which are still competitive, but of course not cutting edge (though still a huge improvement over the pairs of seats currently on the planes).

The 787-9s will really become the next-generation flagship planes for the airline, though some patience will be required. The expectation is that the first of these Dreamliners will be retrofitted in the next 18 to 24 months (so hopefully by some point in 2028), and then it’ll likely take a couple of years for the fleet to be upgraded.

We’ll talk more about the new business class product as such in a bit, but the idea is that the 787-9s will get business class suites, including a front row “business class plus” product. On top of that, the 787-9s will be getting a premium economy cabin for the first time.

The plane will also have up to 70% more premium seats than before. Currently, Aeromexico’s 787-9s have 36 business class seats, while the retrofitted planes will have a total of 61 premium seats, between business class and premium economy. So I suspect the business class cabin won’t actually get that much bigger, but instead, most of that premium addition will come in the form of the new premium economy cabin.

It’s also worth mentioning that Aeromexico is adopting some Delta-style branding, as Delta owns a 20% stake in Aeromexico, and the two airlines have a close partnership.

Aeromexico’s new premium products will be known as Premier One Suites Plus (the “business class plus” product), Premier One Suites (business class), and Premier (premium economy). It seems the 787-8 business class will just be branded as Premier One, given the lack of suites with doors. That all sure seems to be inspired by the Delta One branding that’s used by the carrier’s partner.

Seth Miller from PaxEx.Aero flags how Aeromexico’s new Boeing 787-9 business class suite is from Recaro, as the airline is reportedly the launch customer for this new product. However, the exact product hasn’t actually been named.

Aeromexico CEO Dr. Andres Conesa unveiled the carrier's new premium economy cabin plus refreshed business class seat at #APEXFTEExpo in Singapore this week.Full teaser video in the story: paxex.aero/first-look-a….#PaxEx$RTX

I believe this might be an evolution of the Recaro R7 product (LATAM’s newest 787 business class), which in and of itself was already an evolution of the Recaro CL6720 product (Iberia’s newest A350 business class).

It seems that what was unveiled earlier this year was the new Recaro R7 Horizon concept, which is the same idea, but with upgraded technology and customization.

I imagine that we’ll learn more in the coming months, as this was an unusual way to unveil a new product. But this does seem to be officially happening, so it’s something to look forward to… down the road.

Aeromexico is planning some big upgrades to its Dreamliners. The Boeing 787-9s will be getting all-new cabins, including new business class suites, plus a premium economy cabin for the first time. There will even be a premium business product in the first row, with the products marketed as Premier One Suites Plus, Premier One Suites, and Premier.

As this happens, the 787-8s will be getting the old reverse herringbone seats from the 787-9s, so that will be a meaningful upgrade as well. You can expect these new cabins to roll out starting at some point in 2028, so some patience will be required. I can’t wait to learn more!

What do you make of Aeromexico’s Dreamliner plans?

#6177. Restored to Calder’s plan, the clouds are spinning again

Sen. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., speaks during a ceremony marking the restoration of Alexander Calder’s Mountains and Clouds sculpture in the Hart Senate Office Building atrium on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

The day after Alexander Calder presented his plan for a public art display in the Hart Building’s nine-story atrium to the Architect of the Capitol, he died.

Fifty years later, Alexander S.C. Rower felt a sense of awe as he stared up at his grandfather’s work, finally restored to what he had envisioned.

“It’s totally phenomenal,” he said, pointing up at the now-moving clouds as he spoke, spinning his finger around. “It’s not entertainment, but it’s trying to emulate naturalness, trying to emulate what nature would do.”

It was a long time coming for Rower, who remembers traveling to the Capitol in his 20s for the original dedication of the Mountains and Clouds sculpture in 1987. The mobile portion stopped rotating as Calder intended in the 1990s, and it was ultimately removed in 2014 after being deemed unsafe by the Architect of the Capitol. Millions of dollars in private philanthropy later, Calder’s clouds are spinning again.

Rower was back on the Hill on Wednesday for an event celebrating the restoration, joining Architect of the Capitol Thomas Austin, Sens. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., Angus King, I-Maine, and James Lankford, R-Okla., and the project’s donors. As the speakers addressed the crowd, the clouds began to speed up slightly. Onlookers gathered on the balconies overlooking the atrium and peeked through office windows. Attendees left with tote bags emblazoned with images of Calder’s art.

According to Rower, who leads the Calder Foundation dedicated to preserving and interpreting his grandfather’s art, the mobile is rotating on a 15-hour cycle that is “totally variable.”

“It can go a little faster; it can go a little slower,” he said. “I told the team today that during lunchtime, I want it to speed up just a little bit because everyone’s going to lunch. There’ll be … a lot of activity passing through, and then right at 2:30, well, let’s make it go quieter.”

It was a labor of love for those involved, and not an inexpensive one. Jon and Kim Shirley funded the $12 million restoration. Because the pieces were so large, they were transported on an extra-wide load truck and driven at a speed of 35 miles per hour from Michigan.

“We had to call every senator or governor that we knew on that route, which went through seven states, to get permissions,” he said. “That was a huge thing to overcome, and it all happened over a weekend. So my wife was actually on the phone with a governor’s wife on Saturday evening. The next day, he called up his Department of Transportation and got a permit.”

Christian Quilici, who helped manage the project on behalf of the Shirleys and said he serves as a liaison between the foundation and Congress, said the hardest part of the project was the size of it.

“We had to tear the wall down on C Street, which nobody really thought of in the beginning,” he said. “Nobody got how big this was until it showed up on their doorstep.”

Quilici said he spent years educating at least 30 different senators about the quest to reunite the mobile with the stationary mountains left behind. Some of the biggest champions were seated in the front row at Wednesday’s event, including Senate Democratic Whip Richard J. Durbin. Absent was Sen. Christopher S. Murphy, D-Conn., who has been away from the Capitol while recovering from a stroke but has been a supporter of the sculpture’s restoration for years, pressing former acting Architect of the Capitol Joseph DiPietro on it at a 2024 Senate Legislative Branch Appropriations budget hearing.

“Is there any chance that before I leave the Senate, or at least before I die, we can get the clouds back up there?” Murphy said at the time.

Padilla read a letter on Wednesday from Murphy, whose state was Calder’s home for much of his life.

“This statue is actually a statement on our democracy, that we have big pieces of monumental art right in the middle of our most important and most iconic government buildings. To get this piece of art restored to how it was designed by the artist, well, that’s good for Connecticut. But I also like to think … it’s good for democracy too,” Murphy’s statement said.

The restoration was funded entirely by donations from the Shirleys, who are prominent Calder collectors, according to Rower.

“It’s very emotional to see the work completed after 10 years of us working so hard with the Architect of the Capitol and Calder Foundation. It’s a very overpowering, overwhelming emotion,” said Kim Shirley.

In addition to helping fund the project, she’s a former Senate staffer who worked in Hart before Calder’s work was installed. Years after her time in the Senate was over, her husband Jon wanted to show her the sculpture, now filling the space she used to walk through every day.

But when the two arrived, the clouds weren’t hanging from the ceiling like they were supposed to be. He called up Rower, who was a friend of his, and said he wanted to get them back to how Calder intended. On Wednesday, the three of them stood together in Hart, looking up.

Technological and engineering advancements allowed for newer, lighter clouds to be built and be safe to hang from the ceiling.

“Before it was like a bulb, it looked like a hoagie sandwich, and now it looks just really sharp, like a razor cutting through space, which was Calder’s intention,” Rower said.

According to Rower, it involved laser-measuring the original model of Mountains and Clouds sitting in a glass case nearby in the Hart atrium. The new clouds, he said, are made of carbon fiber.

“These are giant things up in the air, and they’re just so gentle and subtle,” he said.

Younger Hill staffers don’t know a time with clouds. But for those who have spent decades in the building, it was a special moment to see them spin, as Lankford told the crowd.

“I can’t tell you how many tour groups that I’ve walked through this building and I pointed to this, and I said it’s only half there, and would take them over to the little model that’s right over here, and say this is what it’s supposed to look like,” said the senator, a former Hill staffer himself.

Standing under his grandfather’s sculpture, Rower found himself quoting the man responsible for it all.

“I find that everything I do, if it is made for a particular spot, is more successful,” he said, gazing up at it.
